episodes.title: 何を教えているの？
episodes.scene: エナジャイザー初日の休み時間です。アキがコーヒーを飲んでいると、オーストラリアのミアさんと、韓国のミンジュンさんが声をかけてきます。
episodes.q: ミアさんのクラスは、何人でしょう。
episodes.a: 26人です。トゥエンティ・シックス、と言っていました。ミンジュンさんのクラスは、30人くらいです。

dialogue.en: Hi! Mind if we join you?
dialogue.ja: こんにちは。いっしょにいいですか。

dialogue.en: Sure, go ahead.
dialogue.ja: どうぞ。

dialogue.en: Thanks! I'm Mia. I'm from Brisbane, in Australia.
dialogue.ja: ありがとう。ミアです。オーストラリアのブリスベンから来ました。

dialogue.en: And I'm Min-jun. I'm from Seoul.
dialogue.ja: ぼくはミンジュンです。ソウルから来ました。

dialogue.en: Nice to meet you. I'm Aki, from Fukuoka, Japan.
dialogue.ja: はじめまして。アキです。日本の福岡から来ました。

dialogue.en: Nice to meet you too, Aki. So, what do you teach?
dialogue.ja: こちらこそ。アキは、何を教えているんですか。

dialogue.en: I teach fourth grade. Almost every subject.
dialogue.ja: 4年生です。ほとんど全部の教科を教えています。

dialogue.en: Oh, nice! I've got Year Three this year. Twenty-six kids, and they've got a lot of energy.
dialogue.ja: いいですね。わたしは今年、3年生です。26人いて、みんなすごく元気です。

dialogue.en: I teach science at a middle school. I've got about thirty students in each class.
dialogue.ja: ぼくは中学校で理科を教えています。どのクラスも、30人くらいです。

dialogue.en: Sorry, thirteen or thirty?
dialogue.ja: すみません、13ですか、30ですか。

dialogue.en: Thirty. Three, zero. It's a pretty big class.
dialogue.ja: 30です。さん、ゼロ。けっこう多いですよ。

dialogue.en: Thirty? Wow. Some days my twenty-six feel like a hundred.
dialogue.ja: 30人ですか。すごい。うちの26人も、日によっては100人いる気がします。

dialogue.en: Ha! Tell me about it.
dialogue.ja: はは、ほんとそれです。

dialogue.en: So, is this your first Energizer, Aki?
dialogue.ja: アキは、エナジャイザーは初めてですか。

dialogue.en: Yes, it's my first time. I'm a little nervous.
dialogue.ja: はい、初めてです。少し緊張しています。

dialogue.en: Me too. But everyone seems really friendly.
dialogue.ja: ぼくもです。でも、みんなすごく親切そうですね。

dialogue.en: Yeah, you're going to love it. Oh, the next session's about to start. Do you want to grab a coffee first?
dialogue.ja: ええ、きっと気に入りますよ。あ、次のセッションがもうすぐ始まります。先にコーヒーを取りに行きませんか。

dialogue.en: Sure. Let's go.
dialogue.ja: いいですね。行きましょう。

sounds.point: ミート・ユー が ミーチャ
sounds.natural: Nice ta meetcha too.
sounds.clear: Nice to meet you too.
sounds.explain: ミート・ユー が つながって、ミーチャ、と聞こえます。トゥー も弱くなって、タ。ナイスタミーチャ、です。

sounds.point: ア・ロット・オブ が アロッタ
sounds.natural: They've got a lotta energy.
sounds.clear: They've got a lot of energy.
sounds.explain: ア・ロット・オブ が ひとかたまりになって、アロッタ、と聞こえます。オブ は、ほとんど消えます。

sounds.point: ウォント・トゥー が ワナ
sounds.natural: Wanna grab a coffee first?
sounds.clear: Do you want to grab a coffee first?
sounds.explain: ウォント・トゥー が、ワナ、になります。前の ドゥー・ユー も省かれて、いきなり ワナ から始まっています。

joke.en: Thirty? Wow. Some days my twenty-six feel like a hundred.

humor.why: 本当は26人なのに、100人いるように感じると、わざと大きく言っています。聞き手は数を信じるのではなく、にぎやかさに共感して笑います。
humor.cue: 本当の数のすぐあとに、ハンドレッドのような大きすぎる数が出てきたら、大げさの冗談です。

aki.en: Some days my class feels like a hundred kids, too.
aki.ja: わたしのクラスも、100人いるように感じる日があります。

talks.en: Hi, I'm Mia. I teach Year Three at a public primary school in Brisbane. I've got twenty-six kids this year, and honestly, they're a really fun group. They're eight and nine years old, so they've got heaps of energy, especially after lunch. Honestly, by two o'clock, I need a nap more than they do. We start every day with a quick check-in. Everyone says how they're feeling, just in one word. It only takes about five minutes, but it makes a big difference. We share a set of Chromebooks with the class next door, so we use them for reading and for writing stories. My favorite subject to teach is science, because the kids love anything messy. Last term we grew beans in the classroom, and they checked them every single morning.
talks.gist: ミアさんは、ブリスベンで3年生26人の担任です。毎朝、ひとことで気持ちを言う時間をとっています。

talks.en: Hello, I'm Min-jun, from Seoul. I teach science at a middle school, so my students are about thirteen to fifteen years old. I teach five classes, and each class has around thirty students. That's a lot of names to remember! I usually learn all hundred and fifty names by February. Then a new school year starts. In my lessons, I try to do at least one experiment every week. The students work in groups of four. They use tablets to take photos and videos of the experiment, and then they share their results on a slide. Some students are really quiet in front of the class, but they write great comments online. So I think technology helps them join in. My goal this year is to let students ask their own questions, not just answer mine.
talks.gist: ミンジュンさんは、ソウルの中学校で理科です。毎週、4人のグループで実験をしています。

talks.en: Hi everyone, I'm Yu-ting. I'm from Taipei, in Taiwan. I teach English and computer science at an elementary school. I see a lot of different classes, from first grade to sixth grade, so every day is different. With the little ones, we sing songs and play games. With the older kids, we do small coding projects. Right now, my sixth graders are making a simple game about recycling. They work in pairs, and they help each other a lot. Sometimes the game doesn't work, and they get kind of frustrated. But when it finally works, they're so proud. That moment is my favorite part of the job. Next month, they're going to show their games to the fourth graders.
talks.gist: ユーティンさんは、台北の小学校で英語と情報です。6年生は、リサイクルのゲームを作っています。

talks.en: Hello! My name is Wei Ling, and I teach math at a primary school in Singapore. My class is Primary Four, so the kids are about ten. There are thirty-two students in my class. In math, I like to use real things. For example, when we learn about fractions, we cut paper pizzas, and sometimes real fruit. The kids remember it much better that way. We also do a lot of talking in math. I ask them, how did you get that answer? And they explain it to a partner. At first, they found it hard. Now they're getting used to it, and some of them explain things better than I do.
talks.gist: ウェイリンさんは、シンガポールで4年生の算数です。分数は、紙のピザを切って学びます。

talks.en: Hi, I'm Carlo. I'm a high school teacher from Manila, in the Philippines. I teach ICT, so, computers and technology. My classes are pretty big, around forty students. So, managing the class can be a challenge, you know? We don't have a device for every student, so they share, usually two or three students to one computer. That's actually not so bad, because they talk and solve problems together. This year, my students are making short videos about their community. They interview people in their neighborhood, and they edit the videos in class. Some of them are really creative. To be honest, I learn a lot from them. It's hard work, but it's never boring.
talks.gist: カルロさんは、マニラの高校で情報です。40人のクラスで、地域の人にインタビューする動画を作っています。

talks.en: Hi, I'm Priya, from Bengaluru, in India. I teach third grade at a private school. I have twenty-eight students, and they're about eight years old. I teach English and social studies. My students love stories, so I use stories for almost everything. When we learn about our city, they talk to their grandparents and bring the stories to class. It's lovely, because the families get involved too. We have a smart board in the classroom, and once a week we use tablets. I'm here because I want to learn simple ways to use Google tools, without making things complicated for the kids. Every Friday, we pick one story and make a short slide about it together.
talks.gist: プリヤさんは、インドのベンガルールで3年生の担任です。英語と社会を、お話を使って教えています。

episodes.title: 数字を聞き取る
episodes.scene: エナジャイザーのグループワークです。台湾のウェイさんと、フィリピンのカルロさんが同じ机に来て、アキの学校のことを聞いてきます。
episodes.q: ウェイさんの高校は、朝なんじに始まるでしょう。
episodes.a: 7時30分です。セブン・サーティ、と言っていました。生徒は900人くらいで、先生は30人くらいです。

dialogue.en: Hi, is this seat free? I'm Wei. I'm from Taichung, in Taiwan.
dialogue.ja: こんにちは。この席、あいていますか。ウェイです。台湾の台中から来ました。

dialogue.en: Sure, go ahead. I'm Aki, from Fukuoka.
dialogue.ja: どうぞ。アキです。福岡から来ました。

dialogue.en: Hi Aki, I'm Carlo. I teach at a high school in Manila.
dialogue.ja: こんにちは、アキ。カルロです。マニラの高校で教えています。

dialogue.en: So Aki, how many students are at your school?
dialogue.ja: アキの学校は、生徒がなんにんいるんですか。

dialogue.en: Hmm, I'm not sure exactly. What about yours?
dialogue.ja: うーん、正確にはわからないです。そちらはどうですか。

dialogue.en: We have about nine hundred students. It's a pretty big school.
dialogue.ja: うちは900人くらいです。けっこう大きい学校です。

dialogue.en: Nine hundred? Wow. Mine's only around six hundred.
dialogue.ja: 900人ですか。すごいですね。うちは600人くらいしかいません。

dialogue.en: Yeah, it's big. I know maybe fifty of their names.
dialogue.ja: そうですね、大きいです。名前は、50人くらいしか覚えていません。

dialogue.en: Fifty? That's pretty good!
dialogue.ja: ごじゅうにん、ですか。それは、けっこうすごいですよ。

dialogue.en: And how many teachers do you have, Wei?
dialogue.ja: ウェイさんのところは、先生がなんにんいるんですか。

dialogue.en: Around thirty, I think.
dialogue.ja: 30人くらいだと思います。

dialogue.en: Sorry, did you say thirteen or thirty?
dialogue.ja: すみません、13と言いましたか。30ですか。

dialogue.en: Thirty. Not thirteen. Three, zero.
dialogue.ja: 30です。13じゃなくて、さんとゼロです。

dialogue.en: What time does your school start, Aki?
dialogue.ja: アキの学校は、なんじに始まるんですか。

dialogue.en: A little after eight. What about yours, Wei?
dialogue.ja: 8時ちょっとすぎです。ウェイさんのところはどうですか。

dialogue.en: Ours starts a lot earlier. Seven thirty.
dialogue.ja: うちはずっと早いです。7時30分です。

dialogue.en: Wait, did you say seven thirty? That's early!
dialogue.ja: えっ、7時30分って言いましたか。早いですね。

dialogue.en: I can get up at six, but I can't think before eight, you know?
dialogue.ja: ぼくは6時には起きられるけど、8時までは頭が働かないんですよね。

dialogue.en: Same here. I need my coffee first.
dialogue.ja: わたしもです。まずコーヒーがないと、だめなんです。

sounds.point: サーティ と サーティーン、強いところ
sounds.natural: Thirty. Not thirteen.
sounds.clear: Thirty. Not thirteen.
sounds.explain: サーティーンは、うしろのティーンが強く、長めに聞こえます。サーティは、前のサーが強く、うしろのティは短く軽く聞こえます。

sounds.point: キャン は弱く、キャント は強く
sounds.natural: I can get up at six, but I can't think before eight.
sounds.clear: I can get up at six, but I can't think before eight.
sounds.explain: できる、のキャンは弱く短くなって、クン、に近い音です。できない、のキャントは強く長めに読まれ、最後のトは消えることもあります。

sounds.point: ディッド・ユー が ディジャ
sounds.natural: Wait, didja say seven thirty?
sounds.clear: Wait, did you say seven thirty?
sounds.explain: ディッド・ユー が つながって、ディジャ、と聞こえます。聞き返すときに、よく出てくる形です。

joke.en: Yeah, it's big. I know maybe fifty of their names.

humor.why: 九百人の学校で、名前を覚えているのは五十人くらいだと、自分の弱いところを先に言っています。先生ならだれでも分かる悩みなので、親しみがわきます。
humor.cue: 自分のことを小さい数で言って、少し笑いながら話していたら、自分を下げる冗談です。

responses.ja: わたしもです。名前はむずかしいですよね。
ごじゅうにん、ですか。それは、けっこうすごいですよ。

aki.en: Names are hard for me. Faces, no problem.
aki.ja: 名前はにがてです。顔ならちゃんと覚えられます。

talks.en: Hi, I'm Wei, and I teach geography at a high school in Taichung, Taiwan. We have about nine hundred students and around thirty teachers. Our school starts early, at seven thirty, so a lot of students look sleepy in my first class. My students are fifteen to seventeen years old, and we study things like maps, climate, and local geography. My favorite part of the year is our field trips. Twice a year, we take students to the mountains or the coast, so they can see the places they read about in the textbook. The students love it too, and they always come back with lots of photos. This year, I'm trying to use more digital maps in class, not just paper ones. I came to this event to see how other teachers use maps and technology together.
talks.gist: ウェイさんは、台中の高校で地理を教えています。生徒は900人くらいで、学校は朝7時30分に始まります。

talks.en: Hi, I'm Carlo, from Manila, in the Philippines. My high school has around six hundred students, so it's not huge, but it's always busy. The building is right next to a main road, so it gets pretty noisy, especially in the morning. Classes start at eight, and most students come by jeepney, a kind of shared minibus, or on foot. We have one computer lab with about fifteen computers, and that's where I teach ICT. With forty students in a class, the room gets really crowded, you know? My favorite place at school is the covered court in the middle. We use it for assemblies, sports, and our school fair once a year. At this event, I want to find simple tools that still work when three students share one computer.
talks.gist: カルロさんの高校は、生徒が600人くらいで、8時に始まります。コンピューター室には、15台くらいのパソコンがあります。

talks.en: Kia ora, I'm Hana, from Auckland, in New Zealand. I teach at a primary school with about three hundred kids. There are twenty-four in my class this year, and they're seven and eight years old. I try to bring Maori culture into everything I teach, not just one lesson a week. We start each morning with a short karakia, and the kids really look forward to it. When we learn about nature, we talk about the Maori names for plants and animals, not just the English ones. I've got one Chromebook between two students, so they work in pairs a lot, and they help each other really well. My favourite thing to teach is storytelling, because the kids love making up their own stories about our local mountains and rivers. I'd love to see how teachers in other countries bring local culture into their lessons.
talks.gist: ハナさんは、オークランドの小学校で24人のクラスの担任です。マオリの文化を毎日の授業に入れていて、朝はカラキアという短いお祈りから始めます。

talks.en: Hello, I'm Arjun, from Pune, in India. I teach physics at a high school, so my students are about sixteen or seventeen years old. I have five classes, and each one has around thirty-five students. So that's about a hundred and seventy-five students every week! And about a hundred and seventy-five different excuses for missing homework. I like to start each topic with a simple question, something they can guess before we do the experiment. For example, before we study forces, I ask them why a rolling ball stops. We don't have a lab for every class, so three science teachers share one lab room. We have to plan it carefully every week. My students use their phones to record slow-motion videos of our experiments, and that works really well for physics. I came here to learn more ways to use simple technology, without expensive equipment.
talks.gist: アルジュンさんは、プーネの高校で物理を教えています。35人くらいのクラスが5つあり、実験室は理科の先生3人で分けて使っています。

talks.en: Hi everyone, I'm Chloe, and I teach English at a secondary school in Hong Kong. My students are in Form One, so they're twelve or thirteen, and I've got about thirty-two in each class. A lot of my students study English outside school too, so the levels in one class can be really different. I try to give them choices. Stronger students can read a harder book, and others can read something easier. Then they share their stories in small groups. We use Google Classroom for almost everything now: homework, feedback, even group projects. Once a month, we do a speaking project. Students record themselves telling a short story, instead of writing it. A lot of quiet students do much better when they can practise first and record it later. I'd like to find more ways to help students feel confident when they speak, not just when they write.
talks.gist: クロエさんは、香港の中学校で英語を教えています。1クラス32人くらいで、月に1回、短いお話を声で録音する活動をしています。

talks.en: Hi, I'm Liam, from Vancouver, in Canada. I teach grade three at an elementary school, so my students are about eight years old. I've got twenty-two kids this year, which is a pretty normal class size for us. School starts at eight forty-five, which is a bit later than a lot of places, I guess. Even so, some of my students still arrive looking like it's five in the morning. Every morning, we do ten minutes of quiet reading before anything else, just to settle everyone down. I've got one Chromebook for every two students, and we use them mostly for reading and simple writing. My favorite subject to teach is math, especially when we use real things, like blocks or coins, instead of just worksheets. This year, my goal is to get students to explain their thinking out loud, not just write the answer. I'd really like to see how school days are different in other countries.
talks.gist: リアムさんは、バンクーバーの小学校で3年生22人の担任です。学校は8時45分からで、毎朝まず10分間、本を読みます。

episodes.title: 朝の案内を聞く
episodes.topic: このイベントで学びたいこと
episodes.scene: エナジャイザーの、ふつかめの朝です。司会のレイチェルさんが、速いアメリカ英語で、きょうの流れを話します。となりのミアさんに、アキが小声で確かめます。
episodes.q: 中級のワークショップは、何時から、どの部屋で始まるでしょう。
episodes.a: 1時30分から、ビー室です。ワン・サーティ、ルーム・ビー、と言っていました。

dialogue.en: Good morning, everyone! Before we get started, let me walk you through today's schedule.
dialogue.ja: おはようございます、みなさん。始める前に、きょうの流れをご案内しますね。

dialogue.en: We're going to kick off with the keynote right here in the main hall, and that runs until about eleven thirty.
dialogue.ja: まずは、このメイン・ホールで基調講演から始めます。11時30分ごろまでです。

dialogue.en: After that, grab a coffee and relax a little bit. Lunch is at twelve.
dialogue.ja: そのあとは、コーヒーでも飲んで、少しゆっくりしてください。昼食は12時です。

dialogue.en: And yes, I saw everyone wake up when I said coffee.
dialogue.ja: そうそう、コーヒーと言ったら、みんな目が覚めましたね。

dialogue.en: Ha! That's so true.
dialogue.ja: はは、ほんとうにそうです。

dialogue.en: Sorry, what did she say?
dialogue.ja: すみません、いま、なんて言っていましたか。

dialogue.en: The keynote goes till eleven thirty. Then there's a short break, and lunch is at twelve.
dialogue.ja: 基調講演は11時30分までです。そのあと短い休憩があって、お昼は12時です。

dialogue.en: Oh, and don't forget, we're taking a group photo at twelve forty-five, right after lunch, just outside the main hall.
dialogue.ja: あ、それから、忘れないでくださいね。昼食のすぐあと、12時45分に集合写真を撮ります。場所は、メイン・ホールを出たところです。

dialogue.en: A group photo? What time?
dialogue.ja: 集合写真ですか。何時ですか。

dialogue.en: Twelve forty-five. Right after lunch.
dialogue.ja: 12時45分です。お昼のすぐあとです。

dialogue.en: Workshops start at one thirty. Room A is beginner, Room B is intermediate, and Room C is advanced.
dialogue.ja: ワークショップは1時30分からです。エー室が初級、ビー室が中級、シー室が上級です。

dialogue.en: If you're not sure where to go, there's a full room list on the board by the entrance. Check it out!
dialogue.ja: どこに行けばいいか分からないときは、入り口のそばのボードに、部屋の一覧があります。見てみてくださいね。

dialogue.en: Sorry, which room is intermediate?
dialogue.ja: すみません、中級はどの部屋ですか。

dialogue.en: Room B. We're both in the intermediate group, right?
dialogue.ja: ビー室です。わたしたち、ふたりとも中級のグループですよね。

dialogue.en: Yes. Room B at one thirty.
dialogue.ja: はい。ビー室で、1時30分ですね。

dialogue.en: Yep. Let's head over together after the photo.
dialogue.ja: ええ。写真のあと、いっしょに行きましょう。

dialogue.en: Thanks, Mia. I'm still learning English.
dialogue.ja: ありがとう、ミアさん。英語はまだ勉強中なんです。

dialogue.en: No worries. She talks really fast! It's a lot to take in.
dialogue.ja: いえいえ。あの人、本当に早口ですね。いっぺんにたくさんで、頭に入りきらないですよね。

sounds.point: ゴーイング・トゥー が ガナ
sounds.natural: We're gonna kick off with the keynote
sounds.clear: We're going to kick off with the keynote
sounds.explain: ゴーイング・トゥー が 短くつまって、ガナ、と聞こえます。キック・オフ もつながって、ウィア・ガナ・キッコフ、に近い音です。

sounds.point: ア・リトル・ビット が アリルビッ
sounds.natural: relax a little bit
sounds.clear: relax a little bit
sounds.explain: リトル の ティー が ら行に近い音になり、アリル、と聞こえます。ビット の終わりの ティー もほとんど聞こえず、アリルビッ、に近い音です。

sounds.point: チェック・イット・アウト が チェキラウ
sounds.natural: Check it out!
sounds.clear: Check it out!
sounds.explain: チェック・イット・アウト が ひとつながりになって、チェキラウ、のように聞こえます。イット の ティー が 次の アウト とつながって、ラウ、に近い音になります。

joke.en: And yes, I saw everyone wake up when I said coffee.

humor.why: コーヒーという言葉で、会場のみんなが目を覚ました、というだれにでも覚えのある場面を言っています。聞き手は自分のことだと感じて笑います。
humor.cue: 話し手が聞き手みんなのことを言って、会場から笑いが起きたら、あるあるの冗談です。

responses.ja: はは、ほんとうにそうです。

aki.en: I caught only one word. Coffee.
aki.ja: ひとつだけ聞き取れました。コーヒーです。

shower.topic_en: What I hope to learn at this event

talks.en: Hi, I'm Jiwoo. I teach at an elementary school in Busan, and I'm really looking forward to this event. I studied in the U.S. for a few years, so I'm always curious how teachers in different places do things. What I really want to learn here is how other teachers keep kids focused for a whole lesson. My students are great, but their attention kind of drops after the first twenty minutes. I've heard a lot about short, hands-on activities, and I want to steal a few good ideas. I'm also hoping to meet teachers from all over and just talk about our everyday classroom problems. Sometimes it helps just to know that other teachers have the exact same struggles. I'm planning to try at least one new activity as soon as I get back to my class.
talks.gist: ジウさんは、プサンの小学校の担任です。子どもが授業の終わりまで集中できる、短い活動のアイデアを探しています。

talks.en: Hey, I'm Sam. I teach English at a secondary school in Wellington, New Zealand. I'm mostly here for the sessions on feedback. I spend hours marking essays and writing comments, and to be honest, I'm not sure it always helps my students improve. Some weekends, I think my red pen works harder than I do. So I want to learn some quicker ways to give feedback that students will actually read and use. I'm also curious how teachers in other countries teach writing, because English classes probably look pretty different depending on where you are. A colleague told me there's a session on getting students to use rubrics themselves, and that sounds like exactly what I need. Another thing I'd like to pick up is how to get quieter students to share their writing out loud. If I take home even one good idea from this event, it'll be worth the trip.
talks.gist: サムさんは、ウェリントンの中学校で英語です。生徒がちゃんと読んで使えるフィードバックを、もっと手早く返したいそうです。

talks.en: Hi everyone, I'm Rosa, from Cebu, in the Philippines. I teach science at an elementary school. What I hope to learn here is how to do more hands-on experiments with the whole class. I've got about thirty kids, and it's not always easy to give everyone a turn. I saw there's a workshop about simple experiments using things you can find at home, and that's exactly what I'm looking for. I also want to learn how other teachers organize group work so that every student actually joins in, not just the confident ones. Right now, a few strong students tend to take over. I'm hoping to bring back some practical ideas, not just theory, so I can try them with my class as soon as possible.
talks.gist: ロサさんは、セブの小学校で理科です。30人ほどのクラスで、全員が参加できる実験やグループ活動のやりかたを探しています。

talks.en: Hello, I'm Ravi. I look after ICT at my school in Singapore. I'm here mostly for the technology sessions, but what I really want to learn is how teachers use these tools in their daily lessons, not just for special projects. It's one thing to set up a new tool, and another thing to get teachers to use it every week. I'm hoping to pick up some simple, practical examples I can share with my colleagues when I get back. I'm also interested in how other schools handle things like shared devices and student accounts, since we're still working that out ourselves. If I can bring back two or three ideas that teachers will actually use, I'll be happy. For me, the best sessions are the ones with real classroom examples, not just slides.
talks.gist: ラヴィさんは、シンガポールの学校で、アイ・シー・ティーの担当です。先生たちがふだんの授業で使える、かんたんな例を持ち帰りたいそうです。

talks.en: Hi, I'm Emily. I'm a special education teacher in Dublin, Ireland. What I hope to learn at this event is how other teachers use technology to support students with different learning needs, not just as an extra tool, but as part of the everyday lesson. I work with a small group of students, and I'm always looking for ways to make instructions clearer, maybe with pictures or short videos instead of just text. I'd love to talk to teachers who've tried something similar, especially anyone working with younger students. I'm also hoping to learn from teachers outside my own country, because sometimes we get stuck doing things the same way. A fresh idea from somewhere completely different can make a real difference for one student, and for me, that's enough.
talks.gist: エミリーさんは、ダブリンの特別支援の先生です。絵や短い動画で、指示をわかりやすくする方法を探しています。

talks.en: G'day, I'm Jack, from Melbourne. I teach maths at a secondary school, and I also help run our local GEG group, so I go to a lot of these events. Honestly, what I hope to learn this time is something I can actually use in my classroom, not just a nice idea that sits in my notes forever. I'm interested in sessions about using data to help students who are falling behind, because that's a real challenge in my classes. I also just enjoy talking to teachers from other countries, comparing notes, and stealing good ideas. I call it professional borrowing. It sounds much better than stealing. No shame in that! If a session's boring, I might sneak off for a coffee, but I always come back for the ones with actual classroom examples. By the end of this event, I just want two or three things I can try with my students straight away.
talks.gist: ジャックさんは、メルボルンの中学校で数学です。教室ですぐ試せるアイデアを、ふたつかみっつ、持って帰りたいそうです。

episodes.title: 相づちとリアクション
episodes.scene: 休憩中に、オーストラリアのジャックさんと、ニュージーランドのハナさんが、アキのテーブルに来ます。うまくいった授業の話を聞きながら、アキは、あいづちで話を広げます。
episodes.q: ジャックさんの授業で、生徒は何を作ったでしょう。
episodes.a: スパゲッティで作った橋です。ブリッジズ・アウト・オブ・スパゲッティ、と言っていました。いちばんじょうぶな橋には、本を2キロ乗せることができました。

dialogue.en: Hey Aki, anyone sitting here?
dialogue.ja: やあ、アキ。ここ、だれか座っていますか。

dialogue.en: No, go ahead. Have a seat.
dialogue.ja: いいえ、どうぞ。座ってください。

dialogue.en: Kia ora, I'm Hana. We were just talking about our lessons this week.
dialogue.ja: キア・オラ、こんにちは。ハナです。ちょうど、今週の授業の話をしていたところなんです。

dialogue.en: Yeah, I had a really good one. My maths class built bridges out of spaghetti.
dialogue.ja: そうそう。ぼくは、すごくいい授業ができたんですよ。数学のクラスで、スパゲッティで橋を作ったんです。

dialogue.en: No way! Spaghetti?
dialogue.ja: えっ、まさか。スパゲッティで、ですか。

dialogue.en: Yep. Honestly, I sort of made it up the night before. Each group had to build one that could hold as much weight as possible.
dialogue.ja: ええ。正直、前の晩の思いつきなんですけどね。グループごとに、できるだけ重いものを乗せられる橋を作ってもらったんです。

dialogue.en: So how much did the best one hold?
dialogue.ja: それで、いちばんよかった橋は、どれくらい乗せられたんですか。

dialogue.en: Two kilos of books! I couldn't believe it.
dialogue.ja: 本を2キロも乗せたんです。信じられませんでしたよ。

dialogue.en: That's amazing. How did the kids react?
dialogue.ja: すごいですね。生徒たちは、どんな反応でしたか。

dialogue.en: They went wild. A couple of them even wanted to build another one at home.
dialogue.ja: もう大さわぎでしたよ。家でもう1つ作りたい、という子まで、なんにんかいました。

dialogue.en: Honestly, it was pasta-bly my best lesson. Sorry, dad joke.
dialogue.ja: 正直、たぶん、いちばんうまくいった授業でした。すみません、おやじギャグです。

dialogue.en: Aw, that's so cool. I had a good one this week too.
dialogue.ja: わあ、いいですね。わたしも今週、いい授業ができたんです。

dialogue.en: Oh, really? What happened?
dialogue.ja: へえ、そうなんですか。どんな授業だったんですか。

dialogue.en: I told them a Maori legend from our area, and they acted it out in groups. I don't know why, but they really loved it.
dialogue.ja: 地元に伝わるマオリの伝説を話して、グループで劇にしてもらったんです。なぜだか分かりませんが、すごく気に入っていました。

dialogue.en: So, Aki, what about you? Any good lessons lately?
dialogue.ja: で、アキはどうですか。最近、いい授業はありましたか。

dialogue.en: Actually, yes. I made a short animation for math. The kids watched it again and again.
dialogue.ja: はい、じつはありました。算数の短いアニメーションを作ったんです。子どもたちが、なんども見返していました。

dialogue.en: Oh, I love that. Some kids need to see it, not just hear it.
dialogue.ja: それ、すてきですね。聞くだけじゃなくて、見ないと分からない子もいますからね。

dialogue.en: Nice one, Aki. Okay, we'd better get to the next session.
dialogue.ja: いいですね、アキ。さて、そろそろ次のセッションに行かないといけませんね。

sounds.point: ワット・アバウト・ユー が ワラバウチュー
sounds.natural: What about you?
sounds.clear: What about you?
sounds.explain: ワット の おわりの ト が、次の ア とつながって、ら行に近い音で聞こえます。アバウト・ユー も つながって、全体で ワラバウチュー に近い音です。

sounds.point: ソート・オブ が ソータ
sounds.natural: I sorta made it up the night before.
sounds.clear: I sort of made it up the night before.
sounds.explain: ソート・オブ が ひとかたまりになって、ソータ、と聞こえます。オブ は、ほとんど聞こえません。

sounds.point: アイ・ドント・ノウ が アイダノウ
sounds.natural: I dunno why, but they really loved it.
sounds.clear: I don't know why, but they really loved it.
sounds.explain: ドント の ト が消え、ドント・ノウ が まとまって、ダノウ に近い音になります。前の アイ も弱くなり、アイダノウ、と一息に聞こえます。

joke.en: Honestly, it was pasta-bly my best lesson. Sorry, dad joke.

humor.why: パスタと、ポッシブリー（たぶん）の音を重ねただじゃれです。自分でダッド・ジョークだと言って、うめき声も笑いに変えています。
humor.cue: ほかの単語に似た、少し変な単語が聞こえて、話し手がダッド・ジョークと言ったら、だじゃれです。

responses.en: Ha! That's such a dad joke.
responses.ja: はは、まさにおやじギャグですね。

aki.en: Sorry, bad joke. I'm not giving up my day job.
aki.ja: すみません、ひどい冗談でした。本業はやめません。

shower.topic_en: A lesson that went really well

talks.en: Hi, it's Mia again, from Brisbane. I want to tell you about a science lesson that went really well. Last term, each group planted bean seeds in a little pot, and the kids made a chart to check them every morning. After about a week, most of the beans were growing, but one group's pot had nothing at all. They were pretty upset about it. So we talked about it as a whole class, and someone noticed the soil in that pot was completely dry. They'd forgotten to water it! The group started watering it every day, and a few days later, a little green sprout finally came up. The whole class cheered. Honestly, that taught them heaps about patience, more than any worksheet could. For the rest of the term, they checked that chart first thing every morning, before I even asked.
talks.gist: ミアさんの理科の授業です。水やりを忘れて芽が出なかった班が、毎日水をやるようにすると芽が出て、クラスのみんなが喜びました。

talks.en: Hi, it's Yu-ting again, from Taipei. My sixth graders are still making their recycling game, but last week we had a test day, and it went really well. Each pair set up their unfinished game on a tablet, and the other students went around and tried every single one. It was kind of like a mini arcade in our classroom. The testers wrote down any problems on sticky notes and left them next to the tablet. Some students tested those games more carefully than they check their homework. A few games had bugs, but their classmates helped fix them on the spot. Some pairs got great ideas, like adding extra points for sorting the trash correctly. By the end, everyone had tried at least five games. Next month, they're going to show the finished games to the fourth graders, and now they really want them to be perfect.
talks.gist: ユーティンさんの6年生は、作っているとちゅうのリサイクルのゲームを、おたがいに試す日をもちました。見つかった不具合は、その場で友だちといっしょに直しました。

talks.en: Hey, I'm Arjun, from Pune, in India. I teach high school physics, and I want to tell you about a lesson on simple machines. We built pulley systems with string and a few cheap plastic pulleys, and the students had to lift a bag of books using as little force as possible. At first, most groups just used one pulley, and it was still pretty hard work. Then one group added a second pulley, and suddenly the bag felt about half as heavy. When they showed the class, everyone wanted to know how they did it. So we stopped and worked through the maths together, right there on the board. One student said it was the first time physics made his life easier. By the end, every group had rebuilt their system, and the room got really loud, in a good way.
talks.gist: アルジュンさんの物理の授業です。滑車を2つにした班が、本の袋を半分くらいの力で持ち上げ、そのしくみをみんなで考えました。

talks.en: Hi, I'm Sophie, from Manchester, in the UK. I'm on the leadership team, so I don't have my own class, and my story's a bit different. This term, we started a reading buddy scheme. Our Year Tens read with the Year Sevens twice a week. Honestly, I wasn't sure it would work. But the first session went really well. The younger kids were so excited to have a big buddy, and the older ones took the job seriously. Some of them even brought bookmarks to give away. One boy who never liked reading much asked if he could keep the same buddy every week. And teachers across the school have noticed the Year Sevens are calmer afterwards, too.
talks.gist: ソフィーさんは学校のリーダー職です。上級生が下級生と週2回、本を読むしくみを始めたら、初回からとてもうまくいきました。

talks.en: Hi, it's Carlo again, from Manila. Remember those community interview videos my students are making? Last month, we had a screening day for the first few, and it went really well. We don't have a big screen, so we used a projector on the classroom wall and closed the curtains. Forty students, all watching each other's work, and honestly, they were so respectful, even when a video had mistakes. One group interviewed a jeepney driver, you know, the colorful jeeps we ride in Manila, and the whole class was cheering by the end. A few students got kind of emotional, actually, because some of the people they interviewed talked about hard times. After the videos, we just talked as a class for a while. It was one of my best days this year.
talks.gist: カルロさんの高校で、先月、地域のインタビュー動画の、最初の数本の上映会をしました。ジプニーの運転手の動画では、クラスのみんなが歓声をあげました。

talks.en: Hi, I'm Jiwoo, from Busan. I studied in the U.S., so I brought back this idea called a morning meeting, where the whole class sits in a circle before lessons start. At first, my students thought it was a little strange, sitting on the floor instead of at their desks. But last week, we had our best morning meeting yet. We were just sharing weekend stories, and one quiet student who almost never talks told a really funny story about her dog. The whole class was laughing, including me. After that, she seemed more comfortable speaking up in class discussions too. It's only ten minutes a day, but I think it's changed how the class feels as a group.
talks.gist: ジウさんは、アメリカで知った朝の会を続けています。ふだん話さない子が犬の話でみんなを笑わせ、その子は授業でも話しやすくなったようです。

episodes.title: ワークショップの指示を聞く
episodes.topic: 授業でのグーグルの道具の使い方
episodes.scene: ワークショップで、イギリスのトレーナー、オリバーさんが、グーグル・ドキュメントやスライドの操作を英語で指示しています。アキは、分からなかった指示を、となりのウェイリンさんに確かめます。
episodes.q: 最初に、何を開くように言われたでしょう。
episodes.a: 新しいグーグル・ドキュメントです。オープナップ・ア・ニュー・グーグル・ドック、と言っていました。共有する相手は、となりの人、つまりウェイリンさんです。

dialogue.en: Right, everyone, go ahead and open up a new Google Doc, then take a look at the screen up here.
dialogue.ja: では、みなさん。新しいグーグル・ドキュメントを開いて、こちらの画面を見てください。

dialogue.en: Sorry, what do we open?
dialogue.ja: すみません、何を開くんですか。

dialogue.en: A new Google Doc. Click New, at the top left, then Google Docs.
dialogue.ja: 新しいグーグル・ドキュメントです。ひだりうえの、新規、を押して、グーグル・ドキュメントを選びます。

dialogue.en: Now, click on the Share button in the top right corner, and share it with the person next to you.
dialogue.ja: 次に、みぎうえのすみにある、共有ボタンをクリックして、となりの人と共有してください。

dialogue.en: Who do we share it with?
dialogue.ja: だれと共有するんですか。

dialogue.en: The person next to you. That's me! You've got to type in my email.
dialogue.ja: となりの人です。つまり、わたしですね。わたしのメールアドレスを入れないといけませんよ。

dialogue.en: Brilliant. Now make sure it says Editor, not Viewer, so your partner can make changes.
dialogue.ja: いいですね。では、閲覧者ではなく、編集者、になっているか確かめてください。そうすれば、相手も書きかえられます。

dialogue.en: Editor. Got it.
dialogue.ja: 編集者ですね。分かりました。

dialogue.en: And if your partner falls asleep, share it with them anyway.
dialogue.ja: もし、パートナーが寝てしまっても、そのまま共有してください。

dialogue.en: Wait, are you joking?
dialogue.ja: あれ、今の冗談ですか？

dialogue.en: Do you use Google tools with your class, Aki?
dialogue.ja: アキは、クラスでグーグルの道具を使っていますか。

dialogue.en: Yes. I use Classroom to hand out and collect work.
dialogue.ja: はい。クラスルームで、課題を配って、集めています。

dialogue.en: Okay, next one. Head over to your Drive and find the workshop folder.
dialogue.ja: はい、次です。ドライブに移って、ワークショップのフォルダを探してください。

dialogue.en: Sorry, which folder?
dialogue.ja: すみません、どのフォルダですか。

dialogue.en: The workshop folder. It's near the top of your Drive.
dialogue.ja: ワークショップのフォルダです。ドライブの上のほうにありますよ。

dialogue.en: Inside, there's a slide template. Click on the three dots next to it, and choose Make a copy.
dialogue.ja: フォルダの中に、スライドのテンプレートがあります。その横の3つの点をクリックして、コピーを作成、を選んでください。

dialogue.en: Don't worry, I'll help if you get stuck.
dialogue.ja: 心配しないで。こまったら手伝いますから。

dialogue.en: Thanks. It's hard to keep up.
dialogue.ja: ありがとう。ついていくのが大変です。

sounds.point: オープン・アップ と テイク・ア・ルック のつながり
sounds.natural: Go ahead and open up a new Google Doc, then take a look at the screen up here.
sounds.clear: Go ahead and open up a new Google Doc, then take a look at the screen up here.
sounds.explain: オープン・アップ が つながって、オープナップ、と聞こえます。テイク・ア・ルック も、テイカルック、とひと続きに聞こえます。

sounds.point: ヘルプ・イフ が ヘルピフ
sounds.natural: Don't worry, I'll help if you get stuck.
sounds.clear: Don't worry, I'll help if you get stuck.
sounds.explain: ヘルプ の おわりの プ が、次の イフ とつながって、ヘルピフ、に近く聞こえます。アイル・ヘルピフ・ユー・ゲット・スタック、とひと続きです。

sounds.point: 語の終わりの アール を読まない
sounds.natural: Head over to your Drive and find the workshop folder.
sounds.clear: Head over to your Drive and find the workshop folder.
sounds.explain: イギリス英語では、オーバー や フォルダー の終わりの アール を、ほとんど読みません。オウヴァ、フォウルダ、のように、軽い ア で終わって聞こえます。

joke.en: And if your partner falls asleep, share it with them anyway.

humor.why: 眠っている人にも共有しておいて、という、ありえない指示を、ふつうの指示と同じまじめな声で言っています。声が変わらないので、中身のおかしさで気づきます。
humor.cue: 声はふつうの指示と同じなのに、言っている中身がありえないときは、無表情の冗談です。

aki.en: My Drive is perfectly tidy. Just kidding.
aki.ja: わたしのドライブは、完ぺきに整理されています。なんてね、冗談です。

shower.topic_en: How I use Google tools in class

talks.en: Hi, I'm Liam, from Vancouver, in Canada. I teach grade three at a public elementary school, and I've got twenty-two kids this year. I use Google Classroom every single day. Each morning, I post the schedule and any assignments there, so everyone knows what to expect. We've got one Chromebook for every two kids, so a lot of our writing in Google Docs happens in pairs. I like that I can leave comments right on their work, instead of handing back a paper covered in red pen. On Fridays, I send out a short Google Form, just three or four questions about what we learned that week. It only takes a few minutes, but it tells me who needs more help before Monday. And when a student's away for a few days, everything's already in Classroom, so their family can see what we did.
talks.gist: リアムさんは、カナダのバンクーバーで3年生22人の担任です。毎朝グーグル・クラスルームで予定を知らせ、金曜日はグーグル・フォームで1週間をふりかえります。

talks.en: Hi, I'm Chloe, and I teach English at a secondary school in Hong Kong. I have five classes, with about thirty-two students in each. That's a lot of essays to mark! For writing, I use Google Docs with all of my classes. Students write their drafts there, and I leave a comment right next to the sentence I'm talking about, so they know exactly what to fix. Some weekends, I think I even dream in comments. For group work, we use Google Slides. Each group gets one slide in a shared file, so I can see everyone's progress at the same time, without opening eight different files. Once a month, my students record themselves telling a short story, and they hand it in on Google Classroom. I also post readings and homework there, so they can check everything from home.
talks.gist: クロエさんは、香港の中学校で英語です。作文にはグーグル・ドキュメントでコメントを付け、グループの活動は、グーグル・スライドの1つのファイルで見ています。

talks.en: Hello, I'm Min-jun, from Seoul. I teach science at a middle school, and I've got five classes, with about thirty students in each. Before every experiment, I send out a short Google Form, so students write down their prediction first. Then, during the experiment, each group of four records their results in a shared Google Sheet, so I can see all the data come in live. After that, they put their results on a slide and explain what happened to the rest of the class. When one group's numbers look strange, everyone can see it right away, and we talk about what might have gone wrong. That's often the best part of the lesson.
talks.gist: ミンジュンさんは、実験の前にグーグル・フォームで予想を書かせ、結果はグループごとにグーグル・シートに記録させています。

talks.en: Hi, I'm Rosa, and I teach science at an elementary school in Cebu, in the Philippines. I've got grade five this year, about thirty kids. I use Google Slides to show short videos and pictures during my lessons, because it's easier than switching between different apps. After a lesson, I give them a quick Google Form, just four or five questions, and the kids answer it in pairs on our class tablets. It's quick, and I can see right away who's still confused. The next morning, I start with the question most of them got wrong. I also post homework on Google Classroom, with a photo of the page, so parents can see what we're working on too.
talks.gist: ロサさんは、フィリピンのセブで5年生の理科です。授業のあとにグーグル・フォームで短く確かめ、次の朝は、まちがいが多かった問題から始めます。

talks.en: Hey, I'm Sam, from Wellington, in New Zealand. I teach English at a secondary school, and one of my classes this year is Year Nine, twenty-six students. They do a lot of peer editing in Google Docs. They read a partner's essay and leave comments, using sentence starters I give them, like, I noticed, and, I wonder. It keeps the feedback kind, but still useful. I collect final essays through Google Classroom, which saves me carrying a huge stack of paper home every weekend. I can also see who hasn't handed anything in yet, so I can remind them before the deadline. For quick reading checks, I use a short Google Form. It marks itself, which saves me heaps of time. Honestly, that form is my favourite colleague.
talks.gist: サムさんは、ニュージーランドのウェリントンで中学校の英語です。作文の下書きは、グーグル・ドキュメントで、たがいにコメントを書き合います。

talks.en: Hi, I'm Priya, from Bengaluru, in India. I teach third grade at a private school, English and social studies. I've got twenty-eight students, and they love stories. Friday is our tablet day, so that's when we use Google tools the most. We pick one story, and the whole class makes a short Google Slides presentation about it together, with a picture and just a few sentences. For social studies, I sometimes send a simple Google Form home, with one question, like, what did your grandparents do for work? The kids ask their families and fill it in together. Then we look at the answers on the smart board. I also keep our slides in a Google Drive folder, so parents can see what their child made.
talks.gist: プリヤさんは、インドのベンガルールで3年生の英語と社会です。金曜日ごとに、お話をクラスみんなでグーグル・スライドにまとめています。

episodes.title: GEGの話をする
episodes.topic: 先生どうしのつながり
episodes.scene: エナジャイザーの休み時間です。メルボルンのジャックさんが、シンガポールのラヴィさんを紹介してくれます。3人で、ジー・イー・ジーの運営について話します。
episodes.q: ジャックさんのジー・イー・ジーは、どれくらいの頻度で集まるでしょう。
episodes.a: 月に1回、オンラインで集まります。ワンス・ア・マンス、と言っていました。年に1回は、対面の大きいイベントもあります。

dialogue.en: Hey, Aki! How's your first Energizer going?
dialogue.ja: やあ、アキ。初めてのエナジャイザーは、どうですか。

dialogue.en: It's great. I'm learning a lot.
dialogue.ja: すごくいいです。学ぶことがたくさんあります。

dialogue.en: Good to hear. This is Ravi. He looks after ICT at his school in Singapore.
dialogue.ja: それはよかった。こちらはラヴィです。シンガポールの学校で、アイ・シー・ティーの担当をしています。

dialogue.en: Hi, Aki. Did you know Jack runs a GEG in Melbourne?
dialogue.ja: こんにちは、アキ。ジャックは、メルボルンでジー・イー・ジーをやっているんですよ。知っていましたか。

dialogue.en: Really? How often does your GEG meet, Jack?
dialogue.ja: そうなんですか。ジャックのジー・イー・ジーは、どれくらいの頻度で集まるんですか。

dialogue.en: We meet online once a month. And once a year, we do a big event in person.
dialogue.ja: 月に1回、オンラインで集まります。それと年に1回、対面で大きいイベントをします。

dialogue.en: Once a month. What do you do at the meetings?
dialogue.ja: 月に1回ですね。集まりでは、何をするんですか。

dialogue.en: Mostly lesson ideas, short workshops, and lots of tips for using Google tools.
dialogue.ja: 授業のアイデアや、短いワークショップが多いですね。グーグルのツールを使うコツも、たくさん出ます。

dialogue.en: And does everyone come every month?
dialogue.ja: それで、みんな毎月来るんですか。

dialogue.en: Not really. Getting people to show up every time is kind of hard.
dialogue.ja: いや、なかなか。毎回みんなに来てもらうのは、けっこう大変です。

dialogue.en: Your chat group's really active, though. Tell him how it works, Ravi.
dialogue.ja: でも、ラヴィのチャットグループは、いつもにぎやかですよね。どうやっているのか、アキに話してあげてください。

dialogue.en: Sure. We just ask quick questions and share slides. No big meetings, so it's easy to keep going.
dialogue.ja: いいですよ。ちょっとした質問をしたり、スライドを共有したりするだけです。大きな会議がないので、続けやすいんです。

dialogue.en: Good idea. I help run a GEG too. It's called GEG Chikuho.
dialogue.ja: いい考えですね。わたしも、ジー・イー・ジーの運営をしています。ジー・イー・ジー・チクホウといいます。

dialogue.en: Oh, nice! How big is it?
dialogue.ja: へえ、いいですね。どれくらいの人数ですか。

dialogue.en: We started in August 2021. Now we have over two hundred members.
dialogue.ja: 2021年の8月に始めました。今は、200人をこえています。

dialogue.en: Wow, that's a big group! What do you all do together?
dialogue.ja: すごい、大きなグループですね。みんなで何をしているんですか。

dialogue.en: We share lesson ideas and run workshops. We also teach each other how to use Gemini.
dialogue.ja: 授業のアイデアを共有して、ワークショップをひらいています。ジェミニの使い方も、教え合っています。

dialogue.en: Nice. We do lesson ideas, workshops, and way too many snacks.
dialogue.ja: いいですね。授業のアイデアとワークショップと、あとおやつが山ほどです。

sounds.point: テル・ヒム が テリム
sounds.natural: Tell him how it works
sounds.clear: Tell him how it works
sounds.explain: ヒム の はじめの息がほとんど落ちて、イム に近くなります。前の テル とつながって、テリム と聞こえます。

sounds.point: フォー が ファ
sounds.natural: lots of tips for using Google tools
sounds.clear: lots of tips for using Google tools
sounds.explain: フォー が弱く短く読まれて、ファ に近い音になります。ティップス・ファ・ユーズィング、とひと続きに聞こえます。

sounds.point: カインド・オブ が カインダ
sounds.natural: is kinda hard
sounds.clear: is kind of hard
sounds.explain: カインド・オブ が ひとつになって、カインダ と聞こえます。オブ の音は、ほとんど消えます。

joke.en: Nice. We do lesson ideas, workshops, and way too many snacks.

humor.why: まじめな活動を二つ並べてから、三つ目でおやつを出して、流れをずらしています。聞き手は三つ目もまじめなものが来ると思っているので、そこで笑います。
humor.cue: 同じ種類の言葉が二つ続いたあと、三つ目だけ場ちがいなものが来たら、三つ目で外す冗談です。

responses.en: Ha! Snacks are the best part.
responses.ja: はは、おやつがいちばん大事ですよね。

aki.en: I teach math, science, and how to find lost pencils.
aki.ja: 算数と理科と、なくした鉛筆の探し方を教えています。

talks.en: Hi, I'm Jack, and I teach maths at a secondary school in Melbourne. A few years ago, I felt kind of lonely, because I was always planning lessons on my own. So I started a GEG in Melbourne. GEG just means Google Educator Group. It's basically teachers helping teachers. We meet online once a month, and we talk about whatever's on our minds that week, sometimes tech, sometimes just how the term is going. Once a year, we get together in person for a bigger event, with food and a proper agenda. Kids love a bit of competition. Teachers too, honestly. I've already started training. Honestly, the hardest part is getting people to come back every single month. Life gets busy, and teachers are tired. But the ones who do show up, they really show up for each other. I've made some close friends through this group, and a few of them I now message more than my old university mates.
talks.gist: ジャックさんは、ひとりで授業を考えるのがさびしくて、メルボルンでジー・イー・ジーを始めました。月に1回オンラインで、年に1回は対面で集まります。

talks.en: Hi, I'm Ravi. I look after ICT at my school in Singapore, so I'm the person everyone calls when something doesn't work. A while back, a few of us ICT teachers from different schools started a small chat group. It's nothing official, just a place to ask quick questions, like, has anyone solved this Chromebook update problem before? We also share templates and slide decks, so we're not all creating the same thing from scratch. Once a term, we try to meet up for coffee and swap stories in person. It's kind of nice to complain to people who actually understand the job. I think every school needs someone in this role, but it can feel lonely without a group like this behind you. Coming to an event like this helps too, because I get to bring new ideas back to my little group.
talks.gist: ラヴィさんは、ほかの学校のアイ・シー・ティー担当の先生たちと、小さなチャットグループを作りました。気軽に質問をしたり、テンプレートを共有したりしています。

talks.en: Kia ora, I'm Hana. I teach at a primary school in Auckland, and I try to bring Maori language and culture into as much of my teaching as I can. At my school, a small group of us meet every fortnight, that's every two weeks, to plan together. We're not all the same year level, but we share ideas about culture, language, and how to make lessons feel more connected to our community. Sometimes an older teacher will teach the rest of us a new word or a song before we start. It's a really simple kind of support, but it makes a big difference in a hard week. Outside of school, I'm also part of an online group for teachers doing similar work around the country. We share resources and just check in on each other, especially at the end of term, when everyone's really tired.
talks.gist: ハナさんは、オークランドの小学校の先生です。2週間に1回、同僚と集まって、いっしょに授業の計画を立てています。

talks.en: Hello, I'm Wei, and I teach geography at a high school in Taichung. It's a big school, with about nine hundred students. At my school, teachers who teach the same subject sit together in one office, so we naturally talk a lot during the day. If someone finds a good video or a new way to explain a map, they usually just turn around and tell the rest of us. We also have a chat group for sharing files, mostly slides and worksheets. Once a semester, younger teachers like me can watch an older teacher's class, and we talk about it together afterward. I used to feel nervous asking questions, but now I think it's normal for teachers to not know everything. That's honestly the biggest thing I've learned from my community here.
talks.gist: ウェイさんは、台中の高校で地理を教えています。同じ教科の先生がひとつの部屋にいるので、ふだんからよく話して、アイデアを教え合っています。

talks.en: Hi, I'm Emily. I work as a special education teacher in Dublin. My job can feel quite lonely sometimes, because every student I support has different needs, so there's no single lesson plan that works for everyone. A few years ago, I joined a small network of special education teachers across the city. We meet online once a month, and honestly, half the time it just feels like therapy. We talk through tricky situations, and someone almost always has an idea that's worked for them before. We also share resources, visual supports, and small tools we've made ourselves. I think without that group, I'd have burnt out by now. Having people who understand the job, without having to explain everything from the start, that's what keeps me going most weeks.
talks.gist: エミリーさんは、ダブリンで特別支援の先生をしています。同じ仕事の先生たちと月に1回オンラインで集まって、困っていることを相談し合っています。

talks.en: Hi, I'm Carlo, from Manila. I teach ICT at a high school, and my classes are big, around forty students, with two or three students sharing one computer. With forty students, the whole call would just be, can you hear me? You know, managing that alone would be tough, so I lean on a group of ICT teachers from schools around the city. We message each other constantly, mostly asking, hey, how did you get this to work with so few devices? Someone always has a trick. Once a month, a few of us meet up after school and just talk about work over dinner. My students are making short interview videos about our neighborhood right now, and honestly, a tip from another teacher in the group is what got that project started. Teaching ICT with so few devices is hard work, you know, but I don't feel like I'm doing it alone.
talks.gist: カルロさんは、マニラの高校でアイ・シー・ティーを教えています。まわりの学校の先生たちと連絡を取り合い、少ない端末で授業をするコツを教え合っています。

episodes.title: スクール・ストックを紹介する
episodes.scene: エナジャイザーの休み時間です。香港のクロエさんと、インドのアルジュンさんに聞かれて、アキが自分の教材サイトを紹介します。
episodes.q: アルジュンさんが、いちばん知りたかったことは何でしょう。
episodes.a: サイトが、本当に無料かどうかです。ディド・ユー・セイ・フリー、と聞き返して、ザッツ・ザ・メイン・シング、と言っていました。

dialogue.en: Aki, can I ask you something? I heard you made a website for teachers.
dialogue.ja: アキ、ちょっと聞いてもいいですか。先生向けのサイトを作ったって聞きました。

dialogue.en: Yes. It's called School Stock.
dialogue.ja: はい。スクール・ストックといいます。

dialogue.en: School Stock? What kind of website is it?
dialogue.ja: スクール・ストック、ですか。どんなサイトなんでしょう。

dialogue.en: It's a free website for teachers. It has lots of worksheets.
dialogue.ja: 先生のための、無料のサイトです。プリントがたくさんあります。

dialogue.en: Wow. Did you make all of them by yourself?
dialogue.ja: へえ。それ全部、ひとりで作ったんですか。

dialogue.en: Yes, just me. I use AI to make them.
dialogue.ja: はい、ひとりです。エーアイを使って作っています。

dialogue.en: Wait, did you say free? Like, totally free?
dialogue.ja: ちょっと待って。いま、無料って言いましたか。お金は、まったくかからないんですか。

dialogue.en: Yes. It's completely free.
dialogue.ja: はい。完全に無料です。

dialogue.en: Really? Okay, that's the main thing I wanted to know.
dialogue.ja: 本当ですか。いちばん知りたかったのは、そこなんです。

dialogue.en: Let me guess, it takes forever to make one page?
dialogue.ja: 当ててみましょうか。1ページ作るのに、ものすごく時間がかかるんじゃないですか。

dialogue.en: Sometimes. I check every page myself.
dialogue.ja: ときどきです。全部のページを、自分で確かめているので。

dialogue.en: Every page? Join the club. I check mine at midnight.
dialogue.ja: 毎ページ、ですか。わたしも同じですよ。うちは、夜中に確かめています。

dialogue.en: Tell me about it.
dialogue.ja: ほんとそれです。

dialogue.en: So what's on it? Just worksheets?
dialogue.ja: それで、何が入っているんですか。プリントだけですか。

dialogue.en: Worksheets, short animations, a digital dictionary, and a digital abacus.
dialogue.ja: プリントと、うごく解説と、デジタル辞典と、デジタルそろばんです。

dialogue.en: That's a lot! Which one's the most popular?
dialogue.ja: たくさんありますね。どれがいちばん、にんきですか。

dialogue.en: The homework worksheets. Teachers use those the most.
dialogue.ja: 宿題プリントです。先生たちが、いちばんよく使っています。

dialogue.en: So we can just print and use them?
dialogue.ja: じゃあ、印刷して、そのまま使えるんですか。

dialogue.en: Yes. You can download and print them.
dialogue.ja: はい。ダウンロードして、印刷できます。

sounds.point: ゼム が弱くなる
sounds.natural: Did you make all of them by yourself?
sounds.clear: Did you make all of them by yourself?
sounds.explain: オール・オブ・ゼム が ひと続きになって、オーラヴゼム に近い音に聞こえます。ゼム は弱く短くなって、エム くらいにしか聞こえないこともあります。

sounds.point: レット・ミー が レミー
sounds.natural: Lemme guess
sounds.clear: Let me guess
sounds.explain: レット の ト が消えて、ミー とつながり、レミー に近い音になります。レミー・ゲス と、ひと息に聞こえます。

sounds.point: アンド が ン
sounds.natural: So we can just print and use them?
sounds.clear: So we can just print and use them?
sounds.explain: アンド が弱くなって、ロックンロール の ン に近い音になります。プリント・アンド・ユーズ が、プリントンユーズ のように、ひと続きに聞こえます。

joke.en: Every page? Join the club. I check mine at midnight.

humor.why: ジョイン・ザ・クラブは、クラブに入って、ではなく、わたしも同じ苦労をしている、という意味の決まり文句です。夜中まで確かめる自分の苦労を、軽く笑いにしています。
humor.cue: 苦労の話のすぐあとに、ジョイン・ザ・クラブと聞こえたら、わたしも同じだよ、という共感の冗談です。

responses.ja: まったくそのとおりです。

aki.en: Join the club. I check mine on Sunday nights.
aki.ja: わたしもです。わたしは日曜の夜に確かめています。

shower.topic_en: How I make and share teaching materials

talks.en: Hi, I'm Chloe, and I teach English at a secondary school in Hong Kong. I make most of my worksheets myself, usually late at night, to be honest. Our English department keeps a shared folder in Google Drive, and every teacher puts their materials there, so we don't all make the same thing twice. That saves so much time, especially before exams. Before I upload anything, I check that it works for all my students, because my classes have a real mix of English levels. So some worksheets have an easier version and a harder version on the same page. Lately I've started using AI to build a first draft, and then I edit it myself before I share it. It's much faster than starting from a blank page every time. I also share our monthly story recording task, so other teachers can try it with their classes.
talks.gist: クロエさんは、香港の中学校の英語の先生です。英語科のフォルダで教材を共有して、やさしい版とむずかしい版のあるプリントも作っています。

talks.en: Hello, I'm Arjun, from Pune, in India. I teach physics, so a lot of my materials are diagrams and practice problems. I usually build my worksheets in Google Docs, and then I share the folder with the two other science teachers who use our lab. We're a small team, just three of us, so sharing saves a lot of work. Before an exam, we write practice questions together, and we check each other's answers. I like using real examples, like a cricket ball or a moving bus, so the numbers feel less random to my students. I also film short slow-motion videos on my phone and put them in the same folder. But honestly, I still print most of my worksheets, because my students like to write out their working by hand. So paper is still pretty important for us.
talks.gist: アルジュンさんは、プーネの高校で物理を教えています。実験室を使う理科の先生3人で、練習問題をいっしょに作って、答えを確かめ合っています。

talks.en: Hi, I'm Wei Ling, and I teach math at a primary school in Singapore. When I make a new worksheet, I think about my thirty-two students first, because they're all a bit different. For fractions, I still use the paper pizza worksheet I made a few years ago, and I update it a little every year. I share my materials with my team through a folder in Google Drive, and they share theirs with me too, so none of us starts from zero. I print most worksheets in color, because the pictures really help my Primary Four students understand the idea. Sometimes a teacher from another school asks to use my worksheets, and I always say yes. It feels good when something I made helps somewhere else too.
talks.gist: ウェイリンさんは、シンガポールで4年生の算数です。分数で使う紙のピザのプリントを、毎年少しずつ直しています。

talks.en: Hello, I'm Sophie, and I'm part of the leadership team at a school in Manchester. My role isn't really about making worksheets myself anymore. It's more about collecting good materials from our teachers and organizing them so everyone can use them. We keep a shared folder in Google Drive, sorted by subject and year group, and I check it every term. Honestly, the hardest part is just getting teachers to actually upload what they make, because everyone's so busy. Lately, I've started offering biscuits for every upload. I try to make it as simple as possible for them. When a new teacher joins us, that folder saves them so much time in their first year. I always tell new staff, you don't have to make everything from scratch, because someone's probably already made a version you can start from.
talks.gist: ソフィーさんは、マンチェスターの学校のリーダー職です。先生たちの教材を集めて、共有フォルダにまとめています。

talks.en: Hi, I'm Liam, and I teach grade three at an elementary school in Vancouver. I make most of my worksheets for my own class, and I post them in Google Classroom, so my students and their parents can find them easily. I keep a shared folder with the other grade three teachers, so we're not all making the same worksheet in the same week. If someone makes something great, we all use it. My kids are eight, so I still print most worksheets, because typing is still hard for them. For some activities, they work on Chromebooks in pairs. I've started using AI for the first draft of a worksheet, and then I check it carefully before I share it with anyone else. Once, an AI first draft gave my third graders a word problem about buying a car. It saves me time, but the checking part is really important.
talks.gist: リアムさんは、バンクーバーで3年生の担任です。同じ学年の先生とフォルダを共有して、同じプリントを別々に作らないようにしています。

talks.en: Hi, I'm Rosa, and I teach grade five science at an elementary school in Cebu. Most of my lessons are hands-on experiments, but I still make a short worksheet to go with almost every lesson. I don't have a lot of time, so I share worksheets with the other science teachers at my school, and we take turns making new ones. We keep them all in one folder in Google Drive, sorted by topic. That way, nobody has to make everything alone every week. I keep my worksheets simple, in black and white, with lots of space. My students love drawing their own pictures of what they see in the experiment, instead of looking at photos. Sharing with my team is really the only way I can keep up.
talks.gist: ロサさんは、セブの小学校で5年生の理科です。理科の先生どうしで、交代でプリントを作っています。

episodes.title: 生成AIと授業
episodes.topic: わたしの教室のエーアイ
episodes.scene: 休憩中に、イギリスのソフィーさんがアキに声をかけます。韓国のミンジュンさんもいっしょに、先生と生徒のジェミニの使い方について話します。
episodes.q: ソフィーさんの学校で、ジェミニを使い始める前に、先生たちが決めたルールは、何でしょう。
episodes.a: 生徒が使う前に、先生がまず自分で試してみる、というルールです。ティーチャーズ・ハフタ・トライ・イット、のように言っていました。

dialogue.en: Hey, Aki, have you got a minute? I wanted to ask how you use Gemini in your classroom.
dialogue.ja: アキ、ちょっといいですか。授業でジェミニをどう使っているか、聞きたくて。

dialogue.en: Sure. Go ahead.
dialogue.ja: いいですよ。どうぞ。

dialogue.en: Do you use it a lot yourself, for planning and things?
dialogue.ja: アキ自身は、授業の準備なんかで、よく使っていますか。

dialogue.en: Yes. I use it to make materials. But I check every page myself.
dialogue.ja: はい。教材づくりに使っています。でも、全部のページを自分で確かめています。

dialogue.en: That's good to hear. We've just started letting our students try it too.
dialogue.ja: それはいいですね。うちでは、生徒にも使わせ始めたところです。

dialogue.en: Same here. But before we started, all our teachers agreed on one rule.
dialogue.ja: うちもです。でも、始める前に、先生たち全員で、ひとつのルールを決めたんです。

dialogue.en: What was it?
dialogue.ja: どんなルールですか。

dialogue.en: Teachers have to try it themselves first, before the students use it.
dialogue.ja: 先生が、まず自分で試してみること。生徒が使うのは、そのあとです。

dialogue.en: That makes sense. But what if a student just asks it to write the whole thing?
dialogue.ja: なるほど。でも、もし生徒が、ジェミニに全部書かせてしまったら、どうしますか。

dialogue.en: That's the big question, isn't it? We're still working on that one.
dialogue.ja: そこが、いちばんの問題ですよね。その点は、まだ話し合いを続けています。

dialogue.en: Maybe we should just ask Gemini.
dialogue.ja: いっそ、ジェミニに聞いてみましょうか。

dialogue.en: I did. It told me to talk to my teacher.
dialogue.ja: 聞きましたよ。先生に相談してください、と言われました。

dialogue.en: Ha! Good advice. In my class, I want the kids to think first.
dialogue.ja: はは、いい答えですね。わたしのクラスでは、子どもたちに、まず自分で考えてほしいんです。

dialogue.en: And then they can ask Gemini?
dialogue.ja: そのあとで、ジェミニに聞いてもいいんですか。

dialogue.en: Right. They do the thinking. Gemini is like a partner to talk to.
dialogue.ja: そうです。考えるのは子どもたちです。ジェミニは、相談相手のようなものです。

dialogue.en: I really like that, because it keeps them thinking instead of just copying.
dialogue.ja: それ、すごくいいですね。ただ写すだけにならずに、考え続けられますから。

dialogue.en: Oh, we should head back. The next session's starting soon.
dialogue.ja: あ、そろそろ戻りましょう。次のセッションがもうすぐ始まります。

dialogue.en: Okay, let's go.
dialogue.ja: はい、行きましょう。

sounds.point: ハヴ・トゥ が ハフタ
sounds.natural: Teachers have to try it themselves first.
sounds.clear: Teachers have to try it themselves first.
sounds.explain: ハヴ の ヴ が、うしろの トゥ につられて フ に近い音になり、ハフタ、と聞こえます。トゥ も弱くなって、タ くらいの音です。

sounds.point: ワット・イフ のつながり
sounds.natural: What if a student just asks it to write the whole thing?
sounds.clear: What if a student just asks it to write the whole thing?
sounds.explain: ワット・イフ が つながって、ワティフ、に近く聞こえます。アメリカやオーストラリアの人だと、ト が ら行に近くなって、ワリフ、と聞こえます。

sounds.point: ビコーズ の ビ が消える
sounds.natural: I really like that, 'cause it keeps them thinking instead of just copying.
sounds.clear: I really like that, because it keeps them thinking instead of just copying.
sounds.explain: ビコーズ の はじめの ビ が消えて、コーズ、や、コズ、と短く聞こえます。ライク・ザット のすぐあとに、コーズ、と続いています。

joke.en: I did. It told me to talk to my teacher.

humor.why: 先生どうしで困っている問題をジェミニに聞いたら、先生に相談してください、と返ってきた、という話です。先生が先生に相談しなさいと言われる、あべこべがおかしいところです。笑いの的は道具のほうなので、だれも傷つけません。
humor.cue: だれかが、アイ・ディド、やってみましたよ、と言ったあとに、思っていたのと反対の答えが続いたら、皮肉の冗談です。

responses.ja: じゃあ、その先生はわたしたちですね。

aki.en: Gemini sent us back to school!
aki.ja: ジェミニに、学校へ戻されましたね。

talks.en: Hi, I'm Sophie. I'm on the leadership team at a secondary school in Manchester. Before we started using Gemini this year, we spent almost a whole staff meeting just talking about it. Not the most exciting meeting, but an important one. We agreed on a few simple rules together, as a whole staff, because I didn't want them to just come from me. The main one is that teachers have to try any activity themselves first, before they give it to a class. That way, if Gemini gets something wrong, we find out before the students do. We also agreed that our youngest students, the Year Sevens, only use it in lessons, with a teacher in the room. Some teachers were a bit worried at first, but having the rules written down made everyone feel more comfortable. Now I keep a short page about it in our shared folder, so new staff can read it in their first week.
talks.gist: ソフィーさんの学校では、先生みんなでジェミニのルールを決めました。クラスで使う前に、先生がまず自分で試します。

talks.en: Hello, I'm Min-jun, from Seoul. I teach science at a middle school, five classes, about thirty students each. This term, a few groups started using Gemini after their experiment, not during it. They type in their results and ask it to explain any pattern they're not sure about. Then they still have to write the explanation themselves, in their own words, and I check it against their data. At first, some students just copied what it said, so now I also ask them to write down one thing they still want to know. That's helped a lot, actually. I still don't let them use it during the experiment itself, because I want them to notice things with their own eyes first. For me, it's a tool for after the thinking, not instead of it.
talks.gist: ミンジュンさんのクラスでは、実験のあとにジェミニを使います。写すだけにならないように、まだ知りたいことをひとつ書かせています。

talks.en: Hi, I'm Mia. I teach Year Three in Brisbane, twenty-six kids, eight and nine years old. Honestly, my students don't really use Gemini themselves yet. They're a bit young for that. I use it a lot myself, though, for planning. If I need a simple reading text about, say, insects, at just the right level for my class, I can get a rough draft in a minute. Then I read it through and fix it up myself. It saves me heaps of time compared to writing everything from scratch. Once, I did let the whole class ask it a question together, on the big screen, just to show them what it is. They thought it was pretty amazing. But for now, it's mostly my tool, not theirs, and I think that's about right for their age.
talks.gist: ミアさんの3年生は、まだ自分でジェミニを使いません。ミアさんが、授業の準備に使っています。

talks.en: Hi, I'm Ravi. I look after ICT at my school in Singapore. When we first turned on Gemini for our teachers, I got a lot of questions, like, can students see each other's chats, or, can I turn it off for one class? My favourite question was, can it mark my essays tonight? So I made a really short guide, just one page, with pictures, and sent it to every teacher. It covers who can use it, and what not to type into it, like students' names or other personal information. I also tried it with a small group of teachers first, before we gave it to everyone. That way, if there was a problem, it was a small one. A few teachers still come to me with questions every week, but it's way fewer than at the start. I think it just takes time and a bit of patience.
talks.gist: ラヴィさんは、ジェミニの使い方を1枚のガイドにまとめました。まず数人の先生だけで試してから、学校全体に広げました。

talks.en: Hi, I'm Priya, from Bengaluru. I teach third grade, English and social studies, twenty-eight students. We use Gemini together, as a class, on the smart board, not on the tablets. Once a week, after we read a story, I ask it a question in front of everyone, like, why did the fox in the story tell a lie? Then we talk about whether the answer sounds right, based on the story we just read. Honestly, they check its work more carefully than their own. The kids love catching it when it gets something wrong. They're so proud when they do. I like that it gives them one more voice to think about, along with their own idea and their partner's idea. For students this young, I want it to be something we question together, not something they use on their own yet.
talks.gist: プリヤさんのクラスでは、スマート・ボードでジェミニを使います。その答えが合っているかを、読んだお話をもとに、みんなで話し合います。

talks.en: Hi, I'm Sam. I teach English at a secondary school in Wellington. My students write a lot of essays, so Gemini came up fast, mostly because a few students handed in work that didn't sound like them at all. Now, before they write a draft, I ask them to plan it on paper first, just a few notes, no typing. Only after that can they ask Gemini for feedback on their plan, not on the whole essay. It can ask them questions back, like, what's your main point here? But they're not allowed to ask it to write sentences for them. I still catch the odd student trying to skip the planning step. When that happens, we just start again from the notes. It's a bit more work for me to check, but the writing feels like theirs again.
talks.gist: サムさんの生徒は、作文を書く前に、まず紙にメモで計画を立てます。ジェミニに聞けるのは、その計画への意見だけで、文章を書かせるのは禁止です。

episodes.title: グループワークの英語
episodes.topic: グループワークの進め方
episodes.scene: ワークショップのグループ活動の時間です。ジウさん、カルロさん、エミリーさんとアキの4人で、係と、話す順番を決めてから、話し合いを始めます。
episodes.q: アキは、時間を見る係と、メモを取る係の、どちらを引き受けたでしょう。
episodes.a: メモを取る係です。はじめは、アイ・キャン・キープ・タイム、と時間を見る係に手をあげました。でも、エミリーさんに頼まれて、アイル・テイク・ノーツ、と引き受けました。

dialogue.en: Okay, let's pick roles before we start. Who's going to keep time, and who wants to take notes?
dialogue.ja: じゃあ、始める前に係を決めましょう。時間を見る係と、メモを取る係、だれがやりますか。

dialogue.en: I can keep time.
dialogue.ja: 時間は、わたしが見ますよ。

dialogue.en: Oh, I've already got a timer open on my phone. Would you mind taking notes instead, Aki?
dialogue.ja: あ、わたし、もうスマホでタイマーを出してあるんです。アキ、かわりにメモを取ってもらってもいいですか。

dialogue.en: No problem. I'll take notes.
dialogue.ja: いいですよ。メモは、わたしが取ります。

dialogue.en: Great. So Emily's keeping time, and Aki's taking notes.
dialogue.ja: いいですね。じゃあ、時間はエミリー、メモはアキですね。

dialogue.en: And today's question is, how do we help quiet kids join in during group work?
dialogue.ja: それで、今日の問いは、これです。グループ活動で、おとなしい子も参加できるようにするには、どうしたらいいか。

dialogue.en: Let's take turns, one idea each. Emily first, then me, then Jiwoo, then Aki.
dialogue.ja: 順番に、ひとり一つずつ案を出しましょう。まずエミリー、次にぼく、それからジウ、最後にアキ。

dialogue.en: Got you. So I'm third.
dialogue.ja: 了解。わたしは3番目ですね。

dialogue.en: Sorry, can you say the order again?
dialogue.ja: すみません、順番をもう一度言ってもらえますか。

dialogue.en: Sure. Emily, then me, then Jiwoo. You're last, Aki.
dialogue.ja: いいですよ。エミリー、ぼく、ジウ。アキは最後です。

dialogue.en: Okay, I'll start. My idea is picture cards. Each child gets a card that shows their job.
dialogue.ja: じゃあ、わたしから。わたしの案は、絵カードです。一人ひとりに、自分の係が分かるカードを渡します。

dialogue.en: Okay, picture cards for each job.
dialogue.ja: はい、係ごとの絵カード、ですね。

dialogue.en: Nice. Can you give me a second? I need to write my idea down first.
dialogue.ja: いいですね。ちょっと待ってもらえますか。自分の案を、先に書いておきたいので。

dialogue.en: Take your time, Carlo. No pressure.
dialogue.ja: ゆっくりでいいですよ、カルロ。プレッシャーはかけません。

dialogue.en: No pressure? Now I feel pressure!
dialogue.ja: プレッシャーはない？ 今、感じてきました。

dialogue.en: Just a quick reminder, we've got five minutes left.
dialogue.ja: ちょっとお知らせです。残り5分です。

dialogue.en: Okay. My idea's simple, you know. Everyone picks a job before they start, so nobody just sits and watches.
dialogue.ja: はい。ぼくの案はシンプルですよ。始める前に、全員が係を選ぶ。そうすれば、座って見ているだけの子がいなくなります。

dialogue.en: Okay. Everyone picks a job first.
dialogue.ja: はい。最初に全員が係を選ぶ、ですね。

sounds.point: ギブ・ミー が ギミー
sounds.natural: Can you gimme a second?
sounds.clear: Can you give me a second?
sounds.explain: ギブ・ミー の ブ が消えて、ギミー、と聞こえます。少し待って、と頼むときによく出てきます。

sounds.point: ガット・ユー が ガッチャ
sounds.natural: Gotcha.
sounds.clear: Got you.
sounds.explain: ガット の ト と ユー が混ざって、ガッチャ、と聞こえます。分かった、了解、という意味でよく使われます。

sounds.point: ジャスト・ア が ジャスタ
sounds.natural: Just a quick reminder.
sounds.clear: Just a quick reminder.
sounds.explain: ジャスト の ト が、次の ア とつながります。ジャスタ・クイック・リマインダー、に近い音です。

joke.en: Take your time, Carlo. No pressure.

humor.why: 考える時間がほしいカルロさんに、ゆっくりでいいよ、プレッシャーはないよ、と言いながら、本当は時間がないことを軽くからかっています。仲間どうしの冗談なので、笑って乗るのがいちばんの返しです。
humor.cue: ノー・プレッシャーのように、やさしい言葉なのに、時間がない場面で言われたら、からかいの冗談です。

responses.en: No pressure? Now I feel pressure!
responses.ja: プレッシャーはない？ 今、感じてきました。

aki.ja: ちょっと、これでも精いっぱいなんです。

talks.en: Hi, I'm Jiwoo, and I teach at an elementary school in Busan. For group work, I usually put four kids in a team, and each one gets a job: a leader, a recorder, a reporter, and a timekeeper. I write the jobs on small cards, so nobody forgets. At first, some kids only wanted to be the leader, but now they take turns every week, so everyone gets a chance to try each job. I also put a simple timer on the board, and when it goes off, the reporter has to share what the group found, even if they're not finished. It's kind of stressful for them at first, but it keeps things moving. My quietest students often do really well as the recorder, because they get to write instead of speaking in front of everyone. I really think a clear job for everyone is the key.
talks.gist: ジウさんは、4人のグループに4つの係を作り、毎週交代させています。おとなしい子は、話すかわりに書けるので、記録の係で力を発揮するそうです。

talks.en: Hi, I'm Carlo, from a high school in Manila. My classes are big, around forty students, and we don't have enough computers, so groups are usually two or three kids per machine. For our community video project, I give each group clear jobs, you know, like one person asks the interview questions, one holds the camera, and one does the editing. They swap jobs partway through, so everyone gets some practice with each skill. Honestly, the biggest challenge is keeping quiet kids from just watching the whole time. So now, before they start, each group has to tell me who's doing what. If someone doesn't have a job yet, I make them pick one right there. It's simple, but it works. Our screening day went really well, and I think this kind of planning is a big reason why.
talks.gist: カルロさんのクラスは40人で、2人か3人のグループで動画を作ります。始める前に、だれが何をするかを、グループごとに報告させています。

talks.en: Hello, I'm Emily. I teach special education in Dublin. For group work, I keep the groups small, usually two or three students, and I give each person a picture card that shows their job, so they don't have to remember it. One card might show a pencil for the writer, and another might show a clock for the timekeeper. I also use a visual timer, so everyone can see how much time is left without me saying it out loud. Some of my students find it hard to wait for their turn to talk, so I use a small object, like a soft ball, and only the person holding it can speak. The soft ball trick works on adults too. I've tried it at staff meetings. It sounds simple, but it really helps. I also think carefully about who works with who, so one child's strengths can help with another child's challenges.
talks.gist: エミリーさんは、係を絵カードで見せ、残りの時間もタイマーで目に見えるようにしています。話していいのは、やわらかいボールを持っている人だけです。

talks.en: Hi, I'm Wei, and I teach geography at a high school in Taichung. For group work, I usually give each group a map or a set of data, and they have to answer one question together, like why a certain city grew so fast. I give everyone a role. One student reads the map, one takes notes, and one keeps time. I like to mix students with different levels in the same group, so they can help each other. Sometimes I let them choose their own groups, but for harder topics, I make the groups myself, so the work is shared more evenly. Here's my favorite trick. At the end, I choose one student from each group to present, and they don't know who until that moment. You've never seen a group study so hard in the last minute. So everyone has to understand the answer, not just the strongest student.
talks.gist: ウェイさんは、グループの全員に係をわりあてています。発表する人は最後にウェイさんが選ぶので、全員が答えを分かっておく必要があります。

talks.en: Kia ora, I'm Hana, from a primary school in Auckland. At our school, we use an idea called tuakana-teina. It means an older student helps a younger one, a bit like a big brother or sister. When we can, my class teams up with an older class, and the older kids help mine with reading. Inside my own class, I mix confidence levels, so a stronger reader can support someone who's still learning. Each group gets a task card, and I ask them to decide together who does what, instead of me deciding for them. At first, that took a long time, but now they're pretty quick at it. I also leave a little time for someone to share a story from their family, if it connects to the topic. It makes group work feel personal, not just about finishing a task.
talks.gist: ハナさんは、年上の子が年下の子を助ける、トゥアカナ・テイナという考え方を取り入れています。係は、グループの子どもたちに自分で決めさせています。

talks.en: Hi, I'm Arjun. I teach physics at a high school in Pune. For group work, especially in the lab, I put students in threes. One sets up the equipment, one records the results, and one checks that the numbers make sense. Three teachers share our one lab, so we can't waste any time, and clear jobs really help. In the pulley lesson I told you about, nobody was just standing around watching. After each experiment, I ask them to switch jobs for the next one, so everyone learns to set up the equipment, not just the confident kids. I also ask each group to write down one question they still have, not just their results. Some of the best class discussions start from those questions.
talks.gist: アルジュンさんは、3人組で実験をさせ、実験のたびに係を交代させています。結果だけでなく、まだ残っている疑問も、ひとつ書かせています。

episodes.title: 評価の話
episodes.topic: 子どもの評価のしかた
episodes.scene: 休み時間に、カナダのリアムさんと、シンガポールのウェイリンさんが、アキを呼びます。話題は、テストや通知表、ルーブリックです。
episodes.q: リアムさんのクラスでは、テストの点は成績の何パーセントでしょう。
episodes.a: 15パーセントくらいです。フィフティーン・パーセント、と言っていました。残りは、プロジェクトと、ふだんの授業での取り組みです。

dialogue.en: Hi, Aki! Come and sit with us. We're talking about report cards.
dialogue.ja: こんにちは、アキ。いっしょに座りませんか。いま、通知表の話をしているんです。

dialogue.en: Oh, report cards. That's a lot of work.
dialogue.ja: ああ、通知表ですか。大変ですよね。

dialogue.en: Yeah, it's report card season for me right now.
dialogue.ja: ええ、ぼくはちょうどいま、通知表の時期なんです。

dialogue.en: Same here. I've written about a million comments this week.
dialogue.ja: うちもです。今週は、コメントを百万個くらい書きました。

dialogue.en: Tell me about it.
dialogue.ja: ほんとそれです。

dialogue.en: How do you decide the grades, Liam?
dialogue.ja: リアムさんは、成績をどうやって決めているんですか。

dialogue.en: In my class, tests are worth about fifteen percent of the final grade.
dialogue.ja: うちのクラスでは、テストは、成績全体の15パーセントくらいです。

dialogue.en: Sorry, fifteen or fifty?
dialogue.ja: すみません、15ですか、50ですか。

dialogue.en: Fifteen. One, five. The rest comes from a couple of projects and everyday classwork.
dialogue.ja: 15です。1と5。残りは、いくつかのプロジェクトと、ふだんの授業での取り組みです。

dialogue.en: Only fifteen? In maths, we have a couple of big tests each term. They count for a lot more.
dialogue.ja: 15だけですか。算数だと、学期ごとに大きなテストが2回くらいあります。テストの割合は、もっとずっと大きいです。

dialogue.en: I see. Do you use rubrics too?
dialogue.ja: なるほど。ルーブリックも使いますか。

dialogue.en: Yeah, for writing. If a kid gets eight out of ten, the rubric shows them why.
dialogue.ja: ええ、作文で使います。10点のうち8点なら、どうして8点なのか、子どもがルーブリックを見て分かるんです。

dialogue.en: At my school, report cards use three levels, not numbers.
dialogue.ja: わたしの学校では、通知表は数字ではなくて、3段階です。

dialogue.en: Oh, interesting! Just three?
dialogue.ja: へえ、おもしろい。3つだけですか。

dialogue.en: Yes. I also collect reflections in Google Forms and read them.
dialogue.ja: はい。それから、ふりかえりをグーグル・フォームで集めて、読んでいます。

dialogue.en: Oh, I do that too, every Friday. Does it take you long to read them?
dialogue.ja: ぼくも、毎週金曜日にやっています。読むのに、時間はかかりますか。

dialogue.en: A bit. But it helps me understand each kid.
dialogue.ja: 少しかかります。でも、ひとりひとりのことがよく分かります。

dialogue.en: That's the best part of assessment, I think.
dialogue.ja: 評価でいちばんいいところは、そこだと思います。

sounds.point: フィフティーン と フィフティ の強さの位置
sounds.natural: Tests are worth about fifteen percent.
sounds.clear: Tests are worth about fifteen percent.
sounds.explain: フィフティーン は、うしろの ティーン が強く、長く聞こえます。フィフティ は、前の フィフ が強く、うしろの ティ は短く弱く聞こえます。

sounds.point: ア・カップル・オブ の オブ が弱い
sounds.natural: The rest comes from a couple of projects.
sounds.clear: The rest comes from a couple of projects.
sounds.explain: ア・カップル・オブ の オブ は、ア に近い弱い音です。アカプラ・プロジェクツ、のように、ひとかたまりで聞こえます。

sounds.point: アウト・オブ が アウラ
sounds.natural: eight outta ten
sounds.clear: eight out of ten
sounds.explain: アウト・オブ が つながって、アウラ、と聞こえます。ト は ら行に近い音で、オブ は ア くらいに弱く聞こえます。

joke.en: Same here. I've written about a million comments this week.

humor.why: 通知表のコメントを百万個書いた、という、ありえない大きな数で、忙しさを伝えています。聞き手は数を信じるのではなく、大変さに共感して笑います。
humor.cue: ミリオンやハンドレッズ・オブのような大きすぎる数が、忙しい話に出てきたら、大げさの冗談です。

aki.en: I have a million things to grade this week.
aki.ja: 今週は、採点するものが百万個あります。

talks.en: Hi, I'm Liam. I teach grade three in Vancouver, Canada. Assessment is a big part of my week right now, because report cards are due soon. In my class, tests aren't worth that much, maybe fifteen percent of the final grade. I care more about how kids improve over time. For writing, I use a simple rubric, out of ten, and I show it to the students before they start, so they know what I'm looking for. Every Friday, we do a quick reflection in Google Forms, and I read through all of them over the weekend. It's a lot of reading, but it tells me who's struggling before the test does. My students also do a couple of projects each term, and those count for a lot. I don't want one bad test day to decide a kid's grade. I wouldn't want my own bad days graded, either.
talks.gist: リアムさんは、バンクーバーで3年生の担任です。テストは成績の15パーセントくらいで、金曜日のふりかえりを全部読んでいます。

talks.en: Hello, I'm Wei Ling, and I teach maths to Primary Four in Singapore. My class has thirty-two students, and we have a couple of big tests each term. But test scores are only part of the grade. I also score their group work with a rubric, usually out of ten, and I explain the score to each group, so it doesn't feel like a mystery. When we do fractions with paper pizzas, I don't just check the answer. I ask them to explain how they cut the pizza, and why. That's part of the score too. At the end of the year, our reports show levels, not just marks, so parents can see the whole picture. I think that's fairer, because some kids understand a lot but don't do well on tests.
talks.gist: ウェイリンさんは、シンガポールで4年生の算数を教えています。グループの活動にもルーブリックで点をつけて、点のわけを、グループごとに説明しています。

talks.en: Hi, I'm Sophie. I'm on the leadership team at a school in Manchester, so I see assessment across the whole school, not just in one class. Every department does it a little differently, and that's something we're working on. In English, students get detailed written feedback. In maths, it's mostly test scores and short quizzes. We're trying to get every department to use a clear mark scheme, a bit like a rubric, so students understand what a good answer actually looks like, not just a number. I also read a couple of full sets of reports each term, just to check they make sense to parents, not just to teachers. My biggest worry isn't the grades themselves. It's whether a student reads their report and knows what to do next. That's the real point of assessment, I think.
talks.gist: ソフィーさんは、マンチェスターの学校の管理職です。子どもが通知表を読んで、次に何をすればいいか分かることを、いちばん大事にしています。

talks.en: Hi, I'm Yu-ting, from Taipei. I teach English and computer science, so assessment looks different in each class.
