With the younger kids, I mostly watch them during class and write down who needs more help. There aren't really any big tests. With the older students, it's different. Right now, my sixth graders are making a game about recycling, and I'm going to grade it with a rubric. Does it work? Is it creative? Can they explain their thinking? Each part gets a score out of ten. For English, I do short quizzes, but they're only a small part of the grade. I care more about whether students can actually use English in a real conversation. At the end of the semester, I write a short comment for each student, not just a score.
talks.gist: ユーティンさんは、台北の小学校で英語と情報を教えています。6年生が作っているゲームは、ルーブリックで点をつけるつもりです。

talks.en: G'day, I'm Jack, from Melbourne. I teach maths at a secondary school, and honestly, assessment's kind of my least favorite part of the job! We give tests, sure, but they're maybe twenty percent of the final grade. The rest comes from classwork, a couple of projects, and a short interview where I ask each student to explain one problem out loud. That one's actually the most useful, because you find out who really understands it, and who just copied the answer. I also use a rubric for group tasks, and I give feedback in class, not just a number on a page. Our reports have a short comment for each subject, plus a grade from A to E. By the last report, I'm running out of nice ways to say good. They take ages to write, but I reckon they're worth it.
talks.gist: ジャックさんは、メルボルンで数学を教えていて、テストは成績の20パーセントくらいです。ひとりずつ問題を口で説明してもらうのが、いちばん役に立つそうです。

talks.en: Hi, I'm Rosa, from Cebu, in the Philippines. I teach science to grade five. For big topics, I give a written test, but it's not the only thing I look at. During experiments, I use a simple rubric to check if students follow the steps safely and record their results properly. That part counts for a lot of the grade too. I try to give a couple of tests each quarter, plus small quizzes along the way, so one bad day doesn't hurt a student too much. When I check test papers, I don't just mark an answer wrong. I write a short note to explain the mistake. At our school, report cards have both a number and a short comment. I think the comment is what parents actually read first.
talks.gist: ロサさんは、セブで5年生の理科を教えています。実験では、手順を安全に守れているかを、ルーブリックで見ています。

episodes.title: 保護者とのやりとり
episodes.scene: 休み時間です。アキは、フィリピンのロサさんと、ニュージーランドのサムさんと、保護者への連絡や面談の話をします。
episodes.q: ロサさんが、保護者との連絡にいちばん使っているものは何でしょう。
episodes.a: グループ・チャットです。ア・グループ・チャット・ウィズ・ペアレンツ、と言っていました。メールより、チャットのほうがすぐ見てもらえるそうです。

dialogue.en: I was up late answering parent emails last night.
dialogue.ja: ゆうべは、遅くまで保護者のメールに返事をしていました。

dialogue.en: Oh, that's a lot of work.
dialogue.ja: それは大変ですね。

dialogue.en: Yeah, a few parents had questions about the school trip.
dialogue.ja: ええ。校外学習のことで、なんにんかの保護者から質問があって。

dialogue.en: What kind of questions?
dialogue.ja: どんな質問ですか。

dialogue.en: Mostly about the time and what to bring.
dialogue.ja: ほとんどが、時間と持ち物のことです。

dialogue.en: Honestly, I mostly use a group chat with parents.
dialogue.ja: 実は、わたしは保護者との連絡、ほとんどグループ・チャットなんです。

dialogue.en: Really? Not email?
dialogue.ja: へえ、メールじゃないんですか。

dialogue.en: Not really. Parents check the chat right away, but emails just sit there.
dialogue.ja: メールは、あまり使いません。チャットならすぐ見てもらえますが、メールは読まれないままなんです。

dialogue.en: But for bigger things, I like to talk to parents face to face.
dialogue.ja: でも、大事な話のときは、保護者と会って話すようにしています。

dialogue.en: What about parent-teacher meetings?
dialogue.ja: 保護者との面談は、どうしていますか。

dialogue.en: We use an online form, so parents can pick a time. Each meeting's about ten minutes.
dialogue.ja: うちの学校では、オンラインのフォームで、保護者に時間を選んでもらっています。1回10分くらいです。

dialogue.en: I just send a few time options in the chat.
dialogue.ja: わたしは、チャットで時間の候補をいくつか送るだけです。

dialogue.en: We use a school app and a paper notebook.
dialogue.ja: わたしの学校では、連絡アプリと、紙の連絡帳を使っています。

dialogue.en: A paper notebook? For messages?
dialogue.ja: 紙のノートですか。連絡に使うんですか。

dialogue.en: Yes. Parents and I write short notes in it.
dialogue.ja: はい。保護者とわたしが、そこに短いメモを書きます。

dialogue.en: You know, that's really nice. It feels more personal.
dialogue.ja: それ、すごくいいですね。気持ちが伝わる感じがします。

dialogue.en: Thanks. But it's a lot of writing!
dialogue.ja: ありがとうございます。でも、書くのが大変なんです。

dialogue.en: Well, paper never asks for a password.
dialogue.ja: まあ、紙は、パスワードを聞かれることはないですからね。

sounds.point: ラスト・ナイト が ラスナイ
sounds.natural: last night
sounds.clear: last night
sounds.explain: ラスト の ト が、ほとんど聞こえなくなります。ナイト の ト も弱くて、ラスナイ、に近い音です。

sounds.point: トーク・トゥー・ペアレンツ が トークタ・ペアレンツ
sounds.natural: talk to parents
sounds.clear: talk to parents
sounds.explain: トゥー が弱く短く読まれて、タ、に近い音になります。トークタ・ペアレンツ、と聞こえます。

sounds.point: ユー・ノウ が ヤノウ
sounds.natural: Y'know, that's really nice.
sounds.clear: You know, that's really nice.
sounds.explain: ユー が弱く短くなって、ヤノウ、に近い音です。話の始めに入れる、つなぎのことばです。

joke.en: Well, paper never asks for a password.

humor.why: 紙のノートの良いところを、まじめな声で、当たり前のことのように言っています。毎日パスワードに困っている先生どうしだから、笑いになります。
humor.cue: 話し手が笑わずに、当たり前のことをまじめに言って、中身がちょっとおかしければ、無表情の冗談です。

aki.ja: 紙は、充電もいりません。

talks.en: Hi, I'm Rosa, and I teach science at an elementary school in Cebu, in the Philippines. For me, working with parents is mostly about staying in touch, a little at a time. I have a group chat for each class, and I use it for quick updates, like reminding them about a test or a trip. Homework goes on Google Classroom, so families can check it any time, even when their child forgets to mention it. Some parents ask a lot of questions, and some are quieter, so now and then I send the quiet ones a short, friendly message. Every quarter, when report cards go home, I meet each family for about ten minutes. I always start with something good the student did, before I talk about anything harder. Parents seem to relax once they hear that first.
talks.gist: ロサさんは、クラスごとのグループ・チャットで連絡しています。面談では、まず子どものよかったことから話します。

talks.en: Hey, I'm Sam, and I teach English at a secondary school in Wellington, New Zealand. Working with parents at this age is a bit different, because the students are older and more independent. I send a short update by email every few weeks, just a few lines about what we're reading in class. For parent-teacher interviews, we use an online form, so families can pick a time that works for them, usually just ten minutes each. Some parents come to every single one, and others I only meet once a year. Honestly, some families are really busy, so sometimes a quick phone call is easier for everyone. I also try to call home when something's going really well, not just when there's a problem. A short good-news call takes two minutes, but parents remember it for a long time.
talks.gist: サムさんは、数週間ごとに短いメールを送っています。問題のときだけでなく、うまくいっているときにも家庭に電話をかけます。

talks.en: Hi, I'm Priya, from Bengaluru, in India. I teach Grade Three, and working with parents is a big part of my week. Every Friday, we make a short slide about a story we read, and I share it with parents in a Google Drive folder, so they can see what their child made that week. For social studies, I sometimes ask students to talk to their grandparents and bring the story back to class, so families get involved without even realizing it. Once a month, we have an open morning, and parents come and sit in the classroom for a lesson. A lot of them are nervous at first, but they relax once the children start explaining things. I think when parents see the classroom, not just hear about it, they trust the school more.
talks.gist: プリヤさんは、毎週つくるスライドを保護者と共有しています。月に一度、保護者に授業を見に来てもらいます。

talks.en: Hello, I'm Min-jun, from Seoul. I teach science at a middle school, so parents aren't in the classroom very often. Most of our contact is through a school messaging app or a short phone call. Before exams, I send a message about what students should study, and how families can help a little at home. After group experiments, I sometimes share a photo from the lesson, so parents can see something specific, not just a grade. We have parent meetings once a semester, and most are quite short, maybe twenty minutes. Some parents want a lot of detail, and some just want to know their child is doing okay. I try to have one clear thing to say, good or difficult, instead of a long list. That way, the conversation stays useful for everyone.
talks.gist: ミンジュンさんは、学校のアプリと電話で連絡しています。面談では、伝えることを1つにしぼります。

talks.en: Hi, I'm Chloe, from Hong Kong. I teach English at a secondary school, and with five classes, keeping every parent updated isn't easy. I post homework and readings on Google Classroom, so at least the basic information is always there for families to check. For students who are struggling, I send a short message home, usually just one or two lines, before it becomes a bigger problem. At my school, Parents' Day is twice a year, and honestly, it's pretty intense, because I only get about five minutes with each family. I try to bring one piece of the student's work, like their writing or a story they recorded, so we have something real to talk about, not just a number. Honestly, I think my students forget my words even faster. Parents seem to remember that piece of work long after they forget what I actually said.
talks.gist: クロエさんは、勉強でつまずいている生徒の家庭に、早めに短いメッセージを送ります。面談では、生徒の作品を1つ持っていって話します。

talks.en: Hi, it's Mia again, from Brisbane. With younger kids, parents are pretty involved, which is lovely, but it also means heaps of messages! Some days, my phone gets more messages than my class gets homework. I send a short update through the school app most weeks, just photos and a few lines about what we've been doing. When we did our bean-growing project, I shared pictures the whole way through, and parents loved watching it grow alongside their kids. Parent-teacher interviews happen twice a year, fifteen minutes each, and I always show a photo or a piece of work first, because it's an easy way to start the conversation. A few parents help out in the classroom once a week, which the kids really love. Honestly, when parents feel like part of the classroom, everything else gets a little easier.
talks.gist: ミアさんは、学校のアプリで、ほぼ毎週、教室の様子を伝えています。面談では、まず写真か作品を見せます。

episodes.title: 特別支援と視覚支援
episodes.topic: 支援が必要な子への手だて
episodes.scene: 休み時間に、ニュージーランドのハナさんと、アイルランドで特別支援の先生をしているエミリーさんが、アキのテーブルに来ます。何度説明しても分からない子を、どう支えるかが話題になります。
episodes.q: エミリーさんが、授業の最初に必ずすることは、何でしょう。
episodes.a: 絵の予定表を見せることです。ビジュアル・スケジュール、と言っていました。授業でやることを絵にして、順番に並べています。

dialogue.en: Hi Aki, mind if we sit here?
dialogue.ja: アキさん、ここ、座ってもいいですか。

dialogue.en: Sure, have a seat.
dialogue.ja: どうぞ、座ってください。

dialogue.en: Hi again, Aki. Good to see you.
dialogue.ja: アキさん、また会えてうれしいです。

dialogue.en: You too, Emily. Do you mind if I ask you both something?
dialogue.ja: こちらこそ。おふたりに、ひとつ聞いてもいいですか。

dialogue.en: Not at all! Go ahead.
dialogue.ja: もちろん。どうぞ。

dialogue.en: Sometimes I explain many times, but some kids still don't understand.
dialogue.ja: 何回説明しても、まだ分からない子がいることがあるんです。

dialogue.en: Oh, I've been there. More talking doesn't always help.
dialogue.ja: ああ、わたしもありました。たくさん話せば分かる、というものでもないんですよね。

dialogue.en: Me too. Sometimes I just talk louder. It doesn't work.
dialogue.ja: わたしもです。つい、声を大きくしてしまいますが、うまくいきません。

dialogue.en: Ha! Same here.
dialogue.ja: はは、わたしもです。

dialogue.en: That's when I switch to pictures. I always start my lessons with a visual schedule.
dialogue.ja: そういうときは、絵に切りかえます。わたしは授業の最初に、いつも絵の予定表を見せています。

dialogue.en: A visual schedule? Every lesson?
dialogue.ja: 絵の予定表ですか。毎回ですか。

dialogue.en: Every single lesson. Pictures of each activity, in order. That way, they know what's coming next.
dialogue.ja: 毎回、かならずです。やることを絵にして、順番に並べます。そうすれば、次に何があるか分かるんです。

dialogue.en: Aki makes short animations for his class. Emily, have you ever tried anything like that?
dialogue.ja: アキさんは、クラスのために短いアニメーションを作っているんですよ。エミリーさんは、そういうのをためしたことはありますか。

dialogue.en: Not really. I mostly use picture cards. What are they like, Aki?
dialogue.ja: あまりないですね。わたしは、ほとんど絵カードです。アキさん、どんなものなんですか。

dialogue.en: They're short moving pictures. Each one shows one step.
dialogue.ja: 短い、動く絵です。ひとつの動画で、ひとつの手順を見せます。

dialogue.en: Oh, I love that. Can the kids watch them again?
dialogue.ja: いいですね。子どもたちは、もう一度見られるんですか。

dialogue.en: Yes, as many times as they want.
dialogue.ja: はい、何回でも見られます。

dialogue.en: So they can keep watching until they get it. That's brilliant.
dialogue.ja: じゃあ、分かるまで何度でも見られるんですね。それ、すばらしいです。

dialogue.en: Thanks. I'd like to try a visual schedule, too.
dialogue.ja: ありがとうございます。わたしも、絵の予定表をやってみたいです。

sounds.point: ゲット・イット が ゲリッ
sounds.natural: So they can keep watching until they get it.
sounds.clear: So they can keep watching until they get it.
sounds.explain: ゲット の ティー が、ら行に近い音になって、ゲリッ、に近く聞こえます。ゲット と イット が、ひとつの語のように つながって聞こえます。

sounds.point: ノット・アット・オール が ノラロール
sounds.natural: Not at all! Go ahead.
sounds.clear: Not at all! Go ahead.
sounds.explain: ノット と アット の ティー が、どちらも ら行に近い音になって、三つの語が ひと続きに聞こえます。ノラロール、に近い音です。

sounds.point: ハヴ・ユー・エヴァー が ハヴュー・エヴァ
sounds.natural: Emily, have you ever tried anything like that?
sounds.clear: Emily, have you ever tried anything like that?
sounds.explain: ハヴ と ユー が つながって、ハヴュー、のように聞こえます。エヴァー の終わりの アール は ほとんど聞こえず、エヴァ、と短く聞こえます。

joke.en: Me too. Sometimes I just talk louder. It doesn't work.

humor.why: 説明が通じないとき、つい声を大きくしてしまう自分を、先に笑っています。先生ならだれでも覚えがあるので、相手も話しやすくなります。
humor.cue: 自分の失敗を話しながら、話し手が少し笑っていたら、自分を下げる冗談です。いっしょに笑うより、わたしも、と返します。

responses.ja: わたしもです。絵が助けになりますよね。

aki.en: My English is a work in progress. Pictures help me, too.
aki.ja: わたしの英語は、まだ工事中です。わたしにも、絵が助けになります。

shower.topic_en: Helping students who need extra support

talks.en: Hi, I'm Emily, from Dublin. I work with a small group of students who all need something different. One boy I support really struggles when I just talk to him. Even short instructions get lost. So every lesson starts with a visual schedule, and then I break each task into pictures, one card for each step. We stick the cards on his desk, and he checks them off as he goes. At first I worried they'd take too long to make, but once they're made, I use them again and again. What really changed things was letting him check the cards by himself, without asking me first. He seems calmer now, and he asks fewer questions, because he can just look. I still explain things out loud too, but the pictures are what he actually uses.
talks.gist: エミリーさんは、授業を絵の予定表から始めて、手順をひとつずつ絵カードにしています。支えている男の子は、カードを自分で見ながら進めるようになり、落ち着いてきたそうです。

talks.en: Kia ora, I'm Hana, from Auckland. This year I've got one student who's really quiet, and at home, her family mostly speaks Maori. At first, she barely joined in during lessons. So I started using more Maori words and pictures from our local area, because they're familiar to her, and slowly she began to join in. Now I pair her with a classmate who checks on her quietly, instead of me asking in front of everyone. My planning group, the one that meets every fortnight, helped me think of this. One teacher suggested pairing students, and another suggested using pictures from our own community instead of ones from a textbook. It's such a small change, but she puts her hand up now, sometimes. I think support doesn't always mean more work. Sometimes it just means something familiar.
talks.gist: ハナさんは、家でマオリの言葉を話す静かな女の子のために、マオリの言葉や地元の絵を授業に入れました。その子は、ときどき手を挙げるようになったそうです。

talks.en: Hey, I'm Arjun, from Pune. I teach high school physics, and one student in my class really struggles with anything on paper, like diagrams and formulas. But give him something to build, and he understands it faster than almost anyone. In our pulley lesson, he was the one who worked out how to add a second pulley, before I even explained it. So now, whenever I introduce something new, I try to give him something to build first, and we go back to the diagram together afterwards. It's not extra work, really, just a different order. I used to think I had to explain something clearly before students could build it. Now I think, for him, building it is the explanation. I still write the formula on the board, just later than before.
talks.gist: アルジュンさんは、図や式が苦手な生徒に、先に物を組み立ててもらってから、いっしょに図に戻ります。教える順番を変えただけだそうです。

talks.en: Hi, I'm Jiwoo, from Busan. Every morning, my class has a morning meeting, sitting together in a circle. There's a boy in my class who almost never speaks up during lessons, even when he knows the answer. But in morning meeting, when we're just sharing something small, he talks more easily. So now, before I ask him a question in front of the class, I sometimes ask him the same thing quietly first, just the two of us, while the others are unpacking their bags. Then in class, he already has the words ready, and he'll say it again for everyone. It sounds like a small trick, but it's made a real difference. I used to think support meant explaining more. Now I think it sometimes means giving a student a chance to practice first, somewhere quieter, before the real moment.
talks.gist: ジウさんは、あまり発言しない男の子に、授業でする質問を、先にふたりだけのときに聞いておきます。すると、みんなの前でも答えを言えるようになったそうです。

talks.en: Hi, I'm Ravi. I look after ICT at my school in Singapore. Teachers often come to me about one particular student, usually someone who struggles to read the text on a worksheet or a slide. My other favourite question is, is it plugged in? My answer is almost always the same. Turn on read-aloud, or add captions to the video. It's a simple setting, but a lot of teachers don't know it's there. Last month, I showed a teacher how to add captions to a recorded lesson, so a student could read along while listening. She told me he was much calmer in class, because he wasn't lost anymore. I really believe most support doesn't need new software. It just needs someone to show you the setting that was already there. Honestly, that's most of my job these days.
talks.gist: ラヴィさんは、読むのが苦手な生徒には、読み上げや字幕の設定をオンにするだけで助けになると話しています。新しいソフトは、たいてい、いらないそうです。

talks.en: Hi, I'm Liam, from Vancouver. I already use Google Classroom every day, but this year I added something new for one student who finds long text really hard to follow. Instead of writing instructions in one big paragraph, I now split them into short steps, with a picture next to each one, right inside the Google Doc. It only takes a few extra minutes when I'm planning. He still reads the words, but the picture tells him he's in the right place, even if he gets stuck on a sentence. Other students started using the pictures too, actually, even though I only made them for him. Honestly, I use them myself when I forget the plan. I didn't expect that part. Now when I plan a lesson, I ask myself if a picture would help, before I even finish writing the instructions.
talks.gist: リアムさんは、長い文が苦手な子のために、指示を短い手順に分けて、それぞれに絵を入れました。その絵を、ほかの子たちも使い始めたそうです。

episodes.title: 昼食の席で
episodes.scene: 昼食の時間です。アキは、カルロさん、ユーティンさん、ジャックさんのテーブルに加わり、ふるさとの食べ物の話をします。
episodes.q: ユーティンさんがすすめた台湾の食べ物は、何でしょう。
episodes.a: ビーフ・ヌードル・スープです。牛肉の入った麺のスープで、タイペイに来たらぜったいに食べてみて、と言っていました。

dialogue.en: Aki, over here! There's a seat next to Jack.
dialogue.ja: アキ、こっちこっち。ジャックの隣があいてますよ。

dialogue.en: Perfect timing, mate. We were just talking about food from home.
dialogue.ja: ちょうどいいところに来ましたね。ふるさとの食べ物の話をしてたんですよ。

dialogue.en: Have you tried the noodles yet, Aki? They're pretty good.
dialogue.ja: アキ、この麺はもう食べてみましたか。けっこうおいしいですよ。

dialogue.en: Careful with those noodles, Aki. I might build a bridge.
dialogue.ja: アキ、その麺には気をつけてください。ぼくが橋をかけたくなります。

dialogue.en: Ha! The spaghetti bridge!
dialogue.ja: はは、スパゲッティの橋ですね。

dialogue.en: They're okay. But nothing beats beef noodle soup back home.
dialogue.ja: まあまあですね。でも、台湾のビーフ・ヌードル・スープには、かないません。

dialogue.en: Sorry, beef what?
dialogue.ja: すみません、ビーフ、なんと言いましたか。

dialogue.en: Beef noodle soup. If you ever come to Taipei, you have to try it.
dialogue.ja: ビーフ・ヌードル・スープです。いつかタイペイに来たら、ぜったいに食べてみてください。

dialogue.en: In Melbourne, we don't really have one famous dish. Maybe meat pies?
dialogue.ja: メルボルンには、これといった名物料理はないんですよね。ミート・パイくらいかな。

dialogue.en: For me, it's adobo. My mom makes the best one, you know.
dialogue.ja: ぼくはアドボですね。母のアドボが、いちばんおいしいんですよ。

dialogue.en: What about you, Aki? What's good in Fukuoka?
dialogue.ja: アキはどうですか。福岡は、何がおいしいんですか。

dialogue.en: Tonkotsu ramen. The soup is made from pork bones.
dialogue.ja: とんこつラーメンです。豚の骨で、スープを作ります。

dialogue.en: Oh, that sounds amazing. Is it spicy?
dialogue.ja: わあ、おいしそう。からいんですか。

dialogue.en: Not really. It's a rich, creamy soup.
dialogue.ja: いいえ、あまり。こってりした、白いスープです。

dialogue.en: Fair enough. Want some chips, Aki? I grabbed way too many.
dialogue.ja: なるほどね。アキ、フライド・ポテト食べますか。取りすぎちゃって。

dialogue.en: Sure, thanks.
dialogue.ja: ありがとう、いただきます。

dialogue.en: Right, I'm grabbing a cup of tea. Anyone else?
dialogue.ja: よし、ぼくは紅茶を取ってきます。ほかにほしい人、いますか。

dialogue.en: Me, please! Milk tea, if they've got any.
dialogue.ja: わたしも、お願いします。ミルク・ティーがあれば。

sounds.point: カップ・オブ が カッパ
sounds.natural: I'm grabbing a cup of tea.
sounds.clear: I'm grabbing a cup of tea.
sounds.explain: カップ・オブ が つながって、カッパ、に近く聞こえます。オブ は弱い ア だけになって、ヴ の音はほとんど目立ちません。

sounds.point: ベスト・ワン が ベスワン
sounds.natural: My mom makes the best one.
sounds.clear: My mom makes the best one.
sounds.explain: ベスト の おわりの ト が ほとんど聞こえず、ベスワン、に近い音です。ト の口の形だけ作って、すぐに ワン に移っています。

sounds.point: ウォント・サム が ウォンサム
sounds.natural: Want some chips, Aki?
sounds.clear: Want some chips, Aki?
sounds.explain: ウォント の ト がほとんど消えて、ウォンサム、に近く聞こえます。サム も弱く、強く聞こえるのは チップス のほうです。

joke.en: Careful with those noodles, Aki. I might build a bridge.

humor.why: 第四回で話した、スパゲッティの橋の話を、昼ごはんのめんで持ち出しています。前の話を知っている人どうしだけで分かるので、仲間らしさが生まれます。
humor.cue: 前の回に出てきた話が、ちがう場面でとつぜん出てきたら、前の話を拾う冗談です。

responses.ja: はは、スパゲッティの橋ですね。

aki.en: Please, no bridges today. I'm hungry.
aki.ja: 今日は、橋はなしでお願いします。おなかがすいているので。

talks.en: Hi, I'm Carlo, from Manila. When people ask about food from my hometown, I always say adobo first. It's chicken or pork cooked in soy sauce, vinegar, and garlic, and every family makes it a little differently. My mom's version is still my favorite, you know. My family eats rice with almost every meal, sometimes three times a day. On weekends, we like the small food stalls near the market. My favorite is pork barbecue on a stick, with a vinegar dip. Actually, one of my students made a short video about those food stalls for his ICT project. He interviewed a few of the owners, and it turned out really well. For me, food is a big part of how we connect with family back home, and I think that's true in a lot of places.
talks.gist: カルロさんのふるさとの味はアドボで、お母さんのがいちばんだそうです。生徒が、いちばの近くの屋台を取材した動画も作りました。

talks.en: Hi everyone, I'm Yu-ting, from Taipei. If you ask me about food from my hometown, I have to say beef noodle soup first. It's a rich soup with soft beef and thick noodles, and almost every neighborhood has its own favorite shop. My family has been going to the same little shop since I was a kid. We also love night markets back home. You can walk around and try so many things, like oyster omelets or stinky tofu. It smells strong, but it tastes great, I promise! My students love talking about night market food more than almost any other topic in English class. Last week, we made a simple menu together, and everyone had to describe their favorite dish. Food is a great way to start a conversation, even with beginners.
talks.gist: ユーティンさんのふるさとの味は、ビーフ・ヌードル・スープです。ナイト・マーケットの食べ物は、英語の授業で生徒がとくに話したがる話題だそうです。

talks.en: G'day, I'm Jack, from Melbourne. Food from my hometown is a bit tricky, because Melbourne's got food from all over the world. But if I had to pick one classic, I'd say a meat pie. You grab one at the footy, I mean the football, add some tomato sauce, and that's basically a Melbourne tradition. We're also really into coffee, maybe too into it, if you ask my wife. There's a good cafe on almost every corner near my school. For lunch, though, most days I just bring a sandwich, nothing fancy. My GEG group did a fun activity once. Everyone shared a family recipe, and we tried to guess where it was from. A few teachers even brought the real thing to our next in-person meetup. Best meeting we've ever had, honestly.
talks.gist: ジャックさんが選ぶメルボルンの定番は、ミート・パイです。先生の集まりで家庭のレシピを見せ合ったら、次の集まりに本物を持ってきた人もいたそうです。

talks.en: Hi, I'm Priya, from Bengaluru. For me, food from my hometown means a proper South Indian breakfast. Soft idli or a crispy dosa, with sambar and coconut chutney on the side. My grandmother still makes the best sambar in the family, and nobody's figured out her exact recipe. In my class, we often talk about food when we're learning new words, because every kid has something to say about it. Last month, my students brought pictures of a dish from home and told the class a little story about it. One girl explained her grandmother's rice recipe so clearly that everyone wanted to try it. I loved seeing them so proud of their own food and their own families. Honestly, it's one of the easiest ways to get quiet students talking.
talks.gist: プリヤさんのふるさとの味は、イドリやドーサの朝ごはんです。生徒が家庭の料理の写真を持ってきて、クラスで紹介しました。

talks.en: Hi, I'm Chloe, from Hong Kong. When I think of food from my hometown, dim sum comes to mind first. Lots of small dishes, and it's always better when you share them with a big group. My family always says, just one more dish. It's never just one more. My family usually goes for dim sum on Sunday mornings, and the restaurant gets pretty crowded and noisy. We also love milk tea back home. It's strong and a little sweet. In my English class, food is actually a great topic for speaking. Last month, for our speaking activity, my students recorded themselves describing a favorite snack, and some of the recordings were really funny. A few students even talked about dishes their grandparents cook. Food is so ordinary for them, but explaining it in English is a real challenge, and they get really into it.
talks.gist: クロエさんのふるさとの味はディム・サム、つまり点心で、日曜の朝に家族で食べに行きます。先月は、生徒が好きなおやつを英語で説明して、録音しました。

talks.en: Hello, I'm Sophie, from Manchester. Food from my hometown isn't especially fancy, if I'm honest, but a proper Sunday roast is still a big deal in a lot of families. Roast beef or chicken, roast potatoes, gravy, and usually some kind of pudding after. That means dessert, by the way. In my family, pudding is not optional. You also can't really talk about food in Manchester without mentioning curry, because there are so many great South Asian restaurants in the city. I'm on the leadership team, so I don't have my own class. But in our reading buddy scheme, the Year Tens and Year Sevens once read recipes together, and then wrote their own. It's a small thing, but it got both age groups talking about something familiar. Food is one of those topics that works for almost any age.
talks.gist: ソフィーさんのふるさとの味は、日曜日のロースト料理です。学校では、10年生と7年生がペアになってレシピを読み、自分たちでも書いたそうです。

episodes.title: ふるさとの紹介
episodes.scene: 休み時間に、ニュージーランドのハナさん、台湾のウェイさんと、おたがいのふるさとの話をします。アキは、福岡のチクホウという地域を紹介します。
episodes.q: ハナさんが育った町から、海までは、なんぷんでしょう。
episodes.a: 自転車で10分くらいです。テン・ミニッツ、と言っていました。学校が終わると、そこで泳いでいたそうです。

dialogue.en: Aki, you said you're from Fukuoka, right? Which part?
dialogue.ja: アキは、福岡出身って言ってましたよね。福岡のどのあたりですか。

dialogue.en: It's an area called Chikuho.
dialogue.ja: チクホウという地域です。

dialogue.en: Chikuho? Sorry, I've never heard of it. Is it far from Fukuoka City?
dialogue.ja: チクホウですか。ごめんなさい、聞いたことがありません。福岡市から遠いんですか。

dialogue.en: Not really. It's about an hour by train.
dialogue.ja: そんなに遠くないです。電車で1時間くらいです。

dialogue.en: Oh, only an hour? That's not far at all. What's it known for?
dialogue.ja: え、たった1時間ですか。ぜんぜん遠くないですね。どんなことで有名なんですか。

dialogue.en: Long ago, it was famous for coal mining.
dialogue.ja: むかしは、炭鉱で有名でした。

dialogue.en: Interesting. I've been to Fukuoka City once, for a conference.
dialogue.ja: へえ、おもしろいですね。福岡市には、研究会で1回いったことがあります。

dialogue.en: Really? What's your hometown like, Wei?
dialogue.ja: そうなんですか。ウェイさんのふるさとは、どんなところですか。

dialogue.en: I grew up in the mountains, about an hour from Taichung. My family grows tea.
dialogue.ja: 台中から1時間くらいの、山の中で育ちました。うちは、お茶を作っています。

dialogue.en: That sounds lovely. I'd love to try your family's tea.
dialogue.ja: すてきですね。ご家族のお茶、飲んでみたいです。

dialogue.en: It's not bad. My mother says it's the best in Taiwan.
dialogue.ja: 悪くはないですよ。母は、台湾でいちばんだと言っていますけど。

dialogue.en: Not bad? I bet it's amazing. What about you, Hana? Where did you grow up?
dialogue.ja: 悪くない？ きっと、すごくおいしいんでしょうね。ハナさんは、どうですか。どこで育ったんですか。

dialogue.en: In a small town north of Auckland. It's pretty quiet. More sheep than people!
dialogue.ja: オークランドの北にある、小さな町です。けっこう静かですよ。人より羊のほうが多いくらいです。

dialogue.en: Is it near the beach?
dialogue.ja: 海の近くですか。

dialogue.en: Yes, it's about ten minutes away by bike. We used to swim there after school.
dialogue.ja: ええ、自転車で10分くらいです。放課後は、よくそこで泳いでいました。

dialogue.en: Ten minutes? That's so close!
dialogue.ja: 10分ですか。すごく近いですね。

dialogue.en: Yeah, we were really lucky.
dialogue.ja: そうなんです。ほんとうに恵まれていました。

dialogue.en: Sounds like a great place to grow up.
dialogue.ja: 子どもが育つには、いいところですね。

sounds.point: ユーズド・トゥ が ユースタ
sounds.natural: We used to swim there after school.
sounds.clear: We used to swim there after school.
sounds.explain: ユーズド・トゥ の ド が消えて、トゥ も弱くなり、ユースタ、に近く聞こえます。ウィ・ユースタ・スイム・ゼア、とひと続きです。

sounds.point: アイヴ・ビーン・トゥ が アイヴビントゥ
sounds.natural: I've been to Fukuoka City once.
sounds.clear: I've been to Fukuoka City once.
sounds.explain: ビーン は、短く弱く読まれて、ビン に近くなります。アイヴ・ビーン・トゥ が ひとつながりになって、アイヴビントゥ のように聞こえます。

sounds.point: アン・アワー が アナワー
sounds.natural: Oh, only an hour?
sounds.clear: Oh, only an hour?
sounds.explain: アワー は、つづりは エイチ から始まりますが、エイチ は読みません。だから前の アン とつながって、オンリー・アナワー のように聞こえます。

joke.en: It's not bad. My mother says it's the best in Taiwan.

humor.why: 自分では、ノット・バッド、悪くない、と小さく言いながら、お母さんはいちばんだと言っている、と続けています。ひかえめな自分と、自慢したいお母さんのちがいで笑います。
humor.cue: ノット・バッドやア・リトルのように小さく言ったあとで、本当はすごいと分かる話が続いたら、控えめの冗談です。

responses.en: Not bad? I bet it's amazing.
responses.ja: 悪くない？ きっとすごくおいしいんですね。
お母さんの言うとおりでしょうね。

aki.en: Fukuoka ramen is not bad. Okay, it's really good.
aki.ja: 福岡のラーメンは、悪くないです。……正直、すごくおいしいです。

talks.en: Kia ora, I'm Hana. I teach in Auckland now, but I actually grew up in a small town north of the city, right by the coast. From our old house, it's about ten minutes to the beach by bike, and my brothers and I used to ride straight there after school. It's a much quieter place than Auckland. There are more sheep than people, honestly! My parents still live there, in the same house, and I try to visit about once a month. It's a two-hour drive, so I usually go on a Friday night and come back on Sunday. My students love hearing about it, especially the sheep. Some of them have never seen a farm animal up close, so when I bring in photos, they ask so many questions.
talks.gist: ハナさんは、オークランドの北にある、海のそばの小さな町で育ちました。家から海まで、自転車で10分くらいでした。

talks.en: Hello, I'm Wei, from Taichung. I grew up in a small town in the mountains, about an hour outside the city, where my family grows tea. As a kid, I helped pick tea leaves on weekends, and I still remember the smell of the fields early in the morning. It's a really quiet place, with just one small school and one shop. Now I teach geography in the city, but I go back to visit my parents almost every month. The drive up into the mountains is beautiful, especially on a clear day. Most of my students grew up in the city, so when we go on our field trip to the mountains, I tell them about my hometown. Some of them are surprised that tea grows on such steep hills.
talks.gist: ウェイさんは、家族がお茶を作っている、山の小さな町で育ちました。今も、ほぼ毎月、実家に帰っています。

talks.en: Hello, I'm Min-jun, from Seoul. I grew up in an apartment near the mountains in the north of the city, so I spent a lot of weekends hiking with my father. Our apartment was small, but the mountain was basically our backyard. These days, I still live in the same part of Seoul, just a short subway ride from where I grew up. My parents live close by too, so I see them often, usually for dinner on Sundays. Seoul has changed a lot since I was a kid. There are more cafes now, and fewer small shops. But the mountains haven't changed at all, and I still go hiking there when I can. Sometimes I take my students to a small hill near our school to look at rocks and plants. I tell them it's good practice for a real mountain. My students don't believe me. My legs don't either.
talks.gist: ミンジュンさんは、ソウルの山の近くで育ちました。今も同じあたりに住んでいて、ときどき生徒と近くの丘で岩や植物を見ます。

talks.en: Hello, I'm Wei Ling, from Singapore. I grew up in a housing block not far from where I teach now, so almost everything around me is familiar. There's a hawker centre just across the road, and my family still eats there most weekends, usually at the same stall my grandmother liked. Everyone in the neighbourhood seems to know each other, at least a little. I remember walking to primary school with a group of kids from my block, and we still keep in touch now, even as adults. My own students live in similar blocks nearby. So when I write math problems about the hawker centre or the bus stop, they know exactly what I mean. I think that's one nice thing about teaching so close to home. I understand their world a little better, because in a way, it's also mine.
talks.gist: ウェイリンさんは、いま教えている学校の近くの団地で育ちました。だから、子どもたちの暮らしが、身近に感じられるそうです。

talks.en: Hi, I'm Emily, from Dublin. I grew up right in the city, in a small house with four brothers and sisters, so it was never quiet. The best thing about our street was the big park at the end of it. We spent every summer evening there, playing until it got dark. I still live in Dublin, about twenty minutes from that street, and I walk past the park whenever I can. Growing up in a big, noisy family taught me a lot, actually. When everyone's talking at once, you learn to notice the one person who isn't. I think that's helped me in this job. With my students, I try to notice the small things, like how someone's sitting, or whether they're having a good day. Sometimes I take my group to a park near our school, and it reminds me of home.
talks.gist: エミリーさんは、ダブリンの町なかの、5人きょうだいのにぎやかな家で育ちました。みんなが話しているときに、話していない子に気づく目は、そこで身についたそうです。

talks.en: Hello, I'm Arjun, from Pune. I grew up right in the middle of the city, above my family's sweet shop, so my childhood was pretty noisy. I used to do my homework at a table behind the counter, listening to customers coming and going all day. During the monsoon, the street outside would flood a little every year, and we'd help carry boxes upstairs. My parents still run the shop, and I live nearby, just a short ride away. I visit most evenings after school. I think my parents like my students more than they like me. Sometimes I sit at that same table and check my students' work, just like when I was a kid doing homework. My students find it funny that their physics teacher grew up above a sweet shop. Some of them even come by to buy sweets after their exams.
talks.gist: アルジュンさんは、プネーの街の真ん中にある、家族のお菓子屋さんの2階で育ちました。今も、学校が終わると、よく店に寄るそうです。

episodes.title: 働き方とゆとり
episodes.scene: エナジャイザーの休憩時間です。アキと、イギリスのソフィーさん、シンガポールのラヴィさんが、先生の忙しさについて話しています。
episodes.q: ラヴィさんの学校では、先生の負担を減らすために、何を始めたでしょう。
episodes.a: 水曜日を、会議をしない日にしました。ウェンズデイ、ノー・ミーティング・デイ、と言っていました。先生が時間どおりに帰れるようにするためです。

dialogue.en: Aki, how's the term going? Busy?
dialogue.ja: アキ、今学期はどうですか。忙しいですか。

dialogue.en: Very busy. I teach almost every subject.
dialogue.ja: とても忙しいです。ほとんど全部の教科を教えているので。

dialogue.en: I can imagine. Honestly, I'm in meetings most of the time.
dialogue.ja: そうでしょうね。わたしは正直、ほとんどいつも会議です。

dialogue.en: Same at my school. But we started something last term that's really helped.
dialogue.ja: うちの学校も同じです。でも、前の学期に始めたことが、すごく役に立っています。

dialogue.en: Oh, what did you start?
dialogue.ja: へえ、何を始めたんですか。

dialogue.en: We made Wednesday a no-meeting day, so teachers can get out on time.
dialogue.ja: 水曜日を、会議をしない日にしたんです。先生たちが時間どおりに帰れるように。

dialogue.en: Wednesday? Oh, that's clever. Does it actually work?
dialogue.ja: 水曜日ですか。それは名案ですね。実際に、うまくいっていますか。

dialogue.en: Mostly, yeah. We still get a bit of extra work sometimes, but it's much better than before.
dialogue.ja: ええ、だいたいは。時々、少し仕事が増えることもありますが、前よりずっといいです。

dialogue.en: Brilliant. We should have a meeting about it.
dialogue.ja: 名案ですね。それについて、会議をしましょう。

dialogue.en: Ha! So true. I like that idea. There's a Japanese word I love. Yutori.
dialogue.ja: はは、ほんとうに。そのアイデア、いいですね。わたしが大事にしている日本語があります。ゆとり、です。

dialogue.en: Yutori? What does that mean?
dialogue.ja: ゆとり、ですか。どういう意味ですか。

dialogue.en: It means breathing room. Time to think, not just to work.
dialogue.ja: ブリージング・ルーム、ひと息つけるすきま、という意味です。働くだけでなく、考える時間のことです。

dialogue.en: Breathing room. I love that.
dialogue.ja: ブリージング・ルーム。いいことばですね。

dialogue.en: When teachers have breathing room, lessons get better.
dialogue.ja: 先生にゆとりがあると、授業がよくなります。

dialogue.en: So true. Saving teachers time is part of my job too.
dialogue.ja: 本当にそうですね。先生の時間を生み出すのも、ぼくの仕事のひとつです。

dialogue.en: Me too. That's why I share my materials for free. So teachers can look forward to tomorrow's lessons.
dialogue.ja: わたしも同じです。だから、教材を無料で公開しています。あしたの授業が、楽しみになるように。

dialogue.en: That's a lovely goal. Right, the break's nearly over. Shall we head back?
dialogue.ja: すてきな目標ですね。さて、そろそろ休憩が終わります。戻りましょうか。

dialogue.en: Sure. Let's go.
dialogue.ja: はい。行きましょう。

sounds.point: モスト・オブ・ザ が モウスタヴザ
sounds.natural: I'm in meetings most of the time.
sounds.clear: I'm in meetings most of the time.
sounds.explain: モスト の ト が オブ につながって、モウスタヴ、とひとかたまりに聞こえます。うしろの ザ も弱く短くなり、モウスタヴザ・タイム、に近い音です。

sounds.point: ゲット・アウト の ト
sounds.natural: so teachers can get out on time
sounds.clear: so teachers can get out on time
sounds.explain: ラヴィさんの ト は ら行にならず、次の アウト とつながって、ゲタウト、に近い音です。アメリカやオーストラリアの人だと、ゲラウト、と ら行に近く聞こえます。

sounds.point: ヘッド・バック が ヘッバック
sounds.natural: Shall we head back?
sounds.clear: Shall we head back?
sounds.explain: ヘッド の おわりの ド が、次の バック にのみこまれて、ヘッバック、に近く聞こえます。ド の音は、ほとんど聞こえません。

joke.en: Brilliant. We should have a meeting about it.

humor.why: 会議のない日を作ったという話に、それについて会議をしましょう、と返しています。会議が多すぎるのは多くの先生に覚えがあるので、笑いになります。
humor.cue: 今聞いた話と正反対のことを、当たり前のように言っていたら、あるあるの冗談です。

aki.en: Is it just me, or are meetings getting longer?
aki.ja: わたしだけですか。会議って、長くなっていませんか。

shower.topic_en: A day in my life as a teacher

talks.en: Hi, I'm Sophie, from Manchester. I'm on the leadership team now, so my day doesn't start with my own class. I usually get in early, around half past seven, and I check my emails before the building gets busy. Once lessons start, I try to walk around and pop into a few classrooms, just to see how things are going. Some days I teach a small group myself, which I really love, because I do miss having my own class. Lunchtime is often a meeting, and there's usually another one after school, about assessment or a new project we're trying. In between, I collect materials that teachers have made, so we can share the good ones across the school. By the end of the day, I've talked to almost every teacher in the building. It's a busy role, but I like being close to what's actually happening in classrooms.
talks.gist: ソフィーさんは、学校のリーダー職です。7時半に学校に来て、教室を回ったり、先生が作った教材を集めたりしています。

talks.en: Hi, I'm Ravi, from Singapore. I look after ICT at my school, so my day starts before the students arrive. I check that the Chromebooks and the Wi-Fi are working properly. Once lessons begin, I get calls from teachers almost every period. It's usually something small, like a login problem or a frozen screen. I don't mind, actually. I like fixing things. Last term, we made Wednesday a no-meeting day, so teachers can get out on time, or use the afternoon to plan without interruptions. It's made a real difference, especially for the newer teachers. On the other days, I usually run a short training session after school, just fifteen minutes, on one simple tool. I keep it small, so it doesn't feel like extra work. At the end of the day, I check the shared drive, just to make sure everything's backed up before I go home.
talks.gist: ラヴィさんは、学校の情報担当です。水曜日を会議なしの日にして、先生が時間どおりに帰れるようにしました。

talks.en: Hi, I'm Mia, from Brisbane. My day starts with twenty-six very energetic eight and nine year olds. We begin with a quick check-in, just one word about how everyone's feeling. Then we move straight into reading and writing. Mid-morning is maths, and after that we have a short break, which I honestly need as much as the kids do. In the afternoon, we often do science, my favourite subject, because there's always something to look at or touch. We share our Chromebooks with the class next door, so we take turns, usually for writing time. After school, I spend about an hour planning and marking, and I try to leave by four thirty. My rule is simple. I don't take marking home. I get heaps done in that hour, so my evenings are actually mine. Well, that's the rule. I break it about once a week.
talks.gist: ミアさんは、ブリスベンで3年生26人の担任です。採点は放課後の1時間ほどですませ、家には持ち帰りません。

talks.en: Hi, I'm Rosa, from Cebu. I teach grade five science, and I've got about thirty kids in my class. Our classes start early, so I'm usually at school before seven. My day is full of small experiments, even simple ones, because the kids remember things much better when they can touch and see them. I use a rubric to check their work during the experiment, not just at the end. That saves me a lot of time later. Around midday, I send quick updates to parents in our group chat, like a reminder about homework or a test. In the afternoon, I often stay a bit later to prepare materials for the next day, because good experiments take time to set up. Our school guard once asked me if I live there. It's a busy schedule, but I love it when the kids ask to do an experiment again.
talks.gist: ロサさんは、セブで5年生の理科です。実験の途中にルーブリックで様子を見るので、あとの手間が減ります。

talks.en: Hey, I'm Sam, from Wellington. I teach English at a secondary school, so my day is mostly reading and writing with teenagers. I teach four classes, and most lessons have some kind of writing task, like an essay, a journal, or peer feedback. The hardest part of my day is still the evening, when I sit down to mark essays. I used to write long comments for every student, and it took hours. So lately, I've been trying something new. I give each student just one thing to fix, and they fix it in class the next day. It's much faster for me, and I think it actually helps them more. Between classes, I try to check in with a few students who seem quiet or stressed, just a short chat. By the time I get home, I'm tired, but it's a good kind of tired.
talks.gist: サムさんは、ウェリントンで中学校の英語です。長いコメントをやめて、ひとりにひとつだけ、直すところを伝えるようにしました。

talks.en: Hi, I'm Jiwoo, from Busan. I teach at an elementary school. Every morning, my class starts with a morning meeting, sitting together in a circle before lessons begin. It only takes about ten minutes, but it sets a nice tone for the day. During group work, each student has a job, like leader or timekeeper, so everyone knows what they're doing. I move around the room a lot, and I try to listen more than I talk. Lunchtime is when I usually catch up on grading, or get materials ready for the afternoon. After school, I sometimes have staff meetings, or I just plan the next day's lessons. To save time, I plan with the teacher next door, and we split the work. It's a full day, but when a quiet student speaks up in morning meeting, it's all worth it.
talks.gist: ジウさんは、プサンの小学校の担任です。毎日を朝の会で始め、授業の準備は、となりのクラスの先生と分担しています。

episodes.title: いっしょに授業をつくろう
episodes.scene: エナジャイザーの会場で、アキが台湾のユーティンさんと韓国のミンジュンさんに、合同授業をもちかけます。年れいのちがいや時差を確かめて、何をするかを決めます。
episodes.q: 3人が、合同授業のテーマに選んだものは何でしょう。
episodes.a: 「わたしたちのクラスのいちにち」です。ア・デイ・イン・アワー・クラス、と言っていました。まずは、あいさつだけの短いビデオ通話から始めます。

dialogue.en: Can I ask you both something? I have an idea.
dialogue.ja: おふたりに、ちょっと聞いてもいいですか。アイデアがあるんです。

dialogue.en: Sure, what's on your mind?
dialogue.ja: いいですよ。何ですか。

dialogue.en: I'd love to connect our classes online. I want my kids to see a bigger world.
dialogue.ja: クラスどうしを、オンラインでつなげたいんです。子どもたちに、もっと広い世界を見てほしくて。

dialogue.en: That sounds great! Should we set up a group chat to plan it?
dialogue.ja: それはいいですね。計画を立てるのに、グループ・チャットを作りましょうか。

dialogue.en: I'm in! But our students are all different ages, right?
dialogue.ja: わたしもやりたいです。でも、わたしたちの生徒は、年れいがばらばらですよね。

dialogue.en: True. Mine are thirteen to fifteen. Yours are younger, aren't they?
dialogue.ja: たしかに。ぼくの生徒は、13さいから15さいです。おふたりのほうは、もっと小さいですよね。

dialogue.en: Mine are nine or ten. Is the gap too big?
dialogue.ja: うちは、9さいか10さいです。差が大きすぎますか。

dialogue.en: Maybe not. It depends on what we do.
dialogue.ja: そうでもないと思います。何をするか次第ですね。

dialogue.en: Good point. Yu-ting, when it's ten a.m. in Seoul, what time is it there?
dialogue.ja: そうですね。ユーティンさん、ソウルが朝の10時のとき、そちらは何時ですか。

dialogue.en: It's nine. We're one hour behind Korea and Japan.
dialogue.ja: 9時です。台湾は、韓国と日本より1時間おそいんです。

dialogue.en: Maybe something simple, like a video about our school day?
dialogue.ja: かんたんなものがいいかもしれません。学校のいちにちを紹介する動画は、どうでしょう。

dialogue.en: I like that! Let's call it "A Day in Our Class."
dialogue.ja: それ、いいですね。タイトルは、「わたしたちのクラスのいちにち」にしましょう。

dialogue.en: That's perfect! Kids of all ages can do that.
dialogue.ja: ぴったりですね。それなら、どの年れいの子でもできます。

dialogue.en: Why don't we start with a short video call, just to say hello?
dialogue.ja: まずは、あいさつだけの短いビデオ通話から始めませんか。

dialogue.en: Sounds good. Let's use Google Meet and Slides.
dialogue.ja: 賛成です。グーグル・ミートと、グーグル・スライドを使いましょう。

dialogue.en: Three schools, one video call. What could possibly go wrong?
dialogue.ja: 3つの学校で、ビデオ通話は1本。うまくいかないはずがないですよね。

dialogue.en: We'll find out!
dialogue.ja: やってみれば、わかりますね。

dialogue.en: Perfect. I can't wait to try this with you both.
dialogue.ja: 決まりですね。おふたりとやるのが、本当に楽しみです。

sounds.point: セット・アップ・ア が セタッパ
sounds.natural: Should we set up a group chat?
sounds.clear: Should we set up a group chat?
sounds.explain: セット・アップ・ア が ひとつながりになって、セタッパ、に近く聞こえます。アメリカの人だと、ト が ら行に近くなって、セラッパ、と聞こえることもあります。

sounds.point: イズ・イット が イズィッ
sounds.natural: What time is it there?
sounds.clear: What time is it there?
sounds.explain: イズ・イット が つながって、イズィッ、に近く聞こえます。イット の ト は ほとんど聞こえないまま、ゼア に続きます。

sounds.point: ドント・ウィー の ト が消える
sounds.natural: Why don't we start with a short video call?
sounds.clear: Why don't we start with a short video call?
sounds.explain: ドント の ト が ほとんど聞こえず、ワイドンウィ、に近く聞こえます。ドン と ウィ が、すき間なくつながります。

joke.en: Three schools, one video call. What could possibly go wrong?

humor.why: 何かまずいことが起きるかな、という言い方で、本当は、きっと何か起きるよ、と言っています。自分たちの計画に向けて言うので、だれも傷つけません。
humor.cue: 計画の説明のすぐあとに、ワット・クッド・ポッシブリー・ゴー・ロングと聞こえたら、うまくいかないかも、という冗談です。

responses.ja: そう言うと、だいたい何か起きますよ。
やってみれば分かります。

aki.en: A live demo and new Wi-Fi. What could possibly go wrong?
aki.ja: 本番の実演に、初めてのワイファイ。何も起きないはずがありません。

talks.en: Hi, I'm Yu-ting, from Taipei. A joint lesson is something I've actually thought about for a while. My sixth graders are almost done with a recycling game in computer class, and I think it would be amazing if another class could play it and give feedback. We could set up a short video call, and my students could explain how the game works, in English. Feedback from real kids in another country would mean so much more than a comment from me. If the other class is far away, the time difference can be tricky, so we'd probably record some parts instead of doing everything live. Even so, just seeing another classroom and hearing a bit of another language would really open their eyes. My younger students could join too, maybe just to say hello and ask simple questions.
talks.gist: ユーティンさんは、6年生が作っているリサイクルのゲームを、ほかの国のクラスに遊んでもらい、感想を聞きたいと考えています。

talks.en: Hello, I'm Min-jun, from Seoul. For a joint lesson, I keep thinking about experiments. My students already work in groups of four and share their results on slides every week. It wouldn't be too hard to add one more step: sharing our results with a class in another country, and comparing them. Maybe we could try the same simple experiment on the same day, and then meet online afterward to talk about what we found. I think my students would take it more seriously if they knew someone outside Korea was going to see their work. It's also good English practice, because they'd need to explain their thinking clearly, not just to me, but to someone they don't know yet. I'd love to try at least one experiment together this year.
talks.gist: ミンジュンさんは、同じ実験を同じ日にやって、結果をオンラインで見せ合いたいと考えています。

talks.en: G'day, I'm Jack, from Melbourne. Honestly, my first thought was maths, but maths can be a bit dry over a video call. So maybe something hands-on instead. Recently, my class built bridges out of spaghetti, and they loved it. I reckon we could send the instructions to another school, and both classes could build a bridge on the same day. Then we compare results on a call. Whose bridge held the most weight, that sort of thing. Kids love a bit of competition. Teachers too, honestly. I've already started training. We'd need to plan the materials carefully, so everyone has roughly the same stuff, even with a time difference to work around. It's not exactly maths on paper, but there's plenty of maths hiding in it, and that's the best kind.
talks.gist: ジャックさんは、両方のクラスでスパゲッティの橋を作って、通話で結果を比べたいと考えています。

talks.en: Hello, I'm Wei Ling, from Singapore. I teach maths to Primary Four, and lately we've been learning fractions with paper pizzas. For a joint lesson, I'd love to connect with another class and compare how we each explain the same idea. Maybe each class could make a short video with a pizza fraction problem, and then the other class tries to solve it. My students are only about ten, so a live call might be a lot for them. Videos feel easier, and we can still write comments to each other afterward. I think it would help them see that maths isn't just numbers on a page. Kids in another country are thinking about the same problem, just in a different classroom.
talks.gist: ウェイリンさんは、ピザを使った分数の問題を動画にして、相手のクラスに解いてもらいたいと考えています。

talks.en: Hi, I'm Carlo, from Manila. For a joint lesson, I keep coming back to the community videos my students already make. Every year, they interview someone in their neighborhood and edit a short video about it, you know. It would be great if a class from another country did something similar. Then we could exchange videos, so both classes could see a bit of everyday life somewhere completely different. My students share devices, two or three to a computer, so a big live call might be tricky to organize. But sending videos back and forth would work well with what we already do, you know? I think seeing another country's neighborhood, through a kid's own camera, is worth more than any textbook page. With forty students, the whole call would just be, can you hear me?
talks.gist: カルロさんは、生徒が地域の人にインタビューした動画を、ほかの国のクラスと交換したいと考えています。

talks.en: Kia ora, I'm Hana, from Auckland. Every morning, my class starts with a short karakia, and we do a lot of storytelling together. For a joint lesson, I'd love for my students to share a story, maybe about our school or our city, and then hear a story back from another class. We could record it first, since a live call at the right time for everyone is hard to arrange. My students are seven and eight, so keeping it simple works best. One short story from each class, with pictures, nothing too long. I think hearing a story from another country, even a short one, would help my students understand that school looks a bit different everywhere. And that's actually kind of exciting for them.
talks.gist: ハナさんは、学校や町のお話を録音して、ほかの国のクラスと聞かせ合いたいと考えています。

episodes.title: 発表を聞いて質問する
episodes.topic: デモ・スラム いちおしのコツ
episodes.scene: デモ・スラムは、ひとり1分で、授業のいちおしのコツを発表する時間です。司会はレイチェルさんで、インドのプリヤさんの発表のあと、アキが手を挙げて質問します。
episodes.q: プリヤさんが紹介したコツは、準備にどれくらい時間がかかるでしょう。
episodes.a: 2分くらいです。アバウト・トゥー・ミニッツ、と言っていました。

dialogue.en: Okay, everyone, welcome back! It's time for our demo slam. Each teacher gets one minute to share their favorite tip.
dialogue.ja: さあ、みなさん、おかえりなさい。デモ・スラムの時間です。先生ひとりにつき1分で、いちおしのコツを紹介してもらいます。

dialogue.en: First up, Priya! Go ahead and tell us your favorite tip.
dialogue.ja: 最初は、プリヤさんです。どうぞ、いちおしのコツを教えてください。

dialogue.en: You've got sixty seconds. Ready? Go!
dialogue.ja: 持ち時間は60秒です。いいですか。はい、どうぞ。

dialogue.en: Oh no, my timer just froze. Okay, I'll count on my fingers.
dialogue.ja: あら、タイマーが止まってしまいました。では、指で数えますね。

dialogue.en: We've all been there.
dialogue.ja: みんな通る道です。

dialogue.en: Thanks, Rachel! Okay, my tip is the story box.
dialogue.ja: ありがとうございます、レイチェルさん。わたしのコツは、お話ボックスです。

dialogue.en: I keep five small objects in an old shoebox, like a spoon or a toy car.
dialogue.ja: 古い靴の箱に、スプーンやおもちゃの車など、小さいものを5つ入れておきます。

dialogue.en: Each child picks one and starts a story with that object.
dialogue.ja: 子どもがひとりひとつ選んで、それを使ってお話を始めます。

dialogue.en: It's very quick to set up, and my students love it.
dialogue.ja: 準備はすぐにできますし、子どもたちも大好きなんです。

dialogue.en: And that's time! Great tip, Priya. Any questions about it?
dialogue.ja: はい、時間です。いいコツでしたね、プリヤさん。このコツについて、質問はありますか。

dialogue.en: Thank you for the great tip. Can I ask a question?
dialogue.ja: すてきなコツをありがとうございました。質問してもいいですか。

dialogue.en: Of course. Go ahead.
dialogue.ja: もちろんです。どうぞ。

dialogue.en: How long does it take to set up?
dialogue.ja: 準備には、どれくらい時間がかかりますか。

dialogue.en: Oh, about two minutes. I just grab the box and go.
dialogue.ja: ああ、2分くらいです。箱を持っていくだけなので。

dialogue.en: Two minutes. Got it, thank you.
dialogue.ja: 2分ですね。わかりました、ありがとうございます。

dialogue.en: Priya, can I ask one more thing? Where do you get the objects?
dialogue.ja: プリヤさん、もうひとつ聞いてもいいですか。箱に入れるものは、どこから集めるんですか。

dialogue.en: Mostly from my kitchen, to be honest! The kids bring things from home, too.
dialogue.ja: 正直に言うと、ほとんどうちの台所からです。子どもたちも、家から持ってきてくれます。

dialogue.en: I love that. Okay, let's give Priya a big round of applause!
dialogue.ja: いいですね。では、プリヤさんに大きな拍手をお願いします。

sounds.point: テル・アス が テラス
sounds.natural: Go ahead and tell us your favorite tip.
sounds.clear: Go ahead and tell us your favorite tip.
sounds.explain: テル・アス が つながって、テラス、と聞こえます。テル の ル が、つぎの アス と ひとつになって、ラス、に近い音になります。

sounds.point: アバウト・イット が アバウリッ
sounds.natural: Any questions about it?
sounds.clear: Any questions about it?
sounds.explain: アバウト の ト が、ら行に近い音になって、アバウリッ、のように聞こえます。イット の最後の ト は、ほとんど聞こえません。

sounds.point: キャン・アイ・アスク が キャナイ・アスク
sounds.natural: Priya, can I ask one more thing?
sounds.clear: Priya, can I ask one more thing?
sounds.explain: キャン・アイ が つながって、キャナイ、と聞こえます。キャン が弱く読まれると、クナイ、に近い音になることもあります。

joke.en: Oh no, my timer just froze. Okay, I'll count on my fingers.

humor.why: タイマーが止まるという小さなトラブルを、指で数えます、と軽く流しています。困った場面を笑いに変えると、会場の空気がやわらかくなります。
humor.cue: 機械が止まったあとで、話し手が明るい声で別のやり方を言ったら、場を和ませる冗談です。

responses.en: That's the story of my life.

aki.en: The projector needs a coffee break. I have a whiteboard.
aki.ja: プロジェクターも休けいが要るみたいです。ホワイトボードがあります。

shower.topic_en: Demo slam: my favorite tip in one minute

talks.en: Hi, I'm Priya, from Bengaluru. My favorite tip is something I call the story box. It's just an old shoebox, and I keep five small objects inside, things like a spoon, a toy car, or a little bell. Before we start a writing lesson, each child picks one object without looking. Then they have to start a story with that object in the first sentence. It sounds simple, but the kids get really excited, because they never know what they'll pick. I change the objects every few weeks, so it stays fresh. The best part is the setup. It only takes about two minutes, because I just keep the box ready by the door. Now my students ask about it before I even bring it out. It's become their favorite part of the week.
talks.gist: プリヤさんのコツは、お話ボックスです。子どもが箱から選んだものでお話を始め、準備は2分ほどで済みます。

talks.en: Hey everyone, I'm Dan. I work for Google for Education, so I go to a lot of these events, and I get to watch hundreds of demos every year. My favorite tip isn't really mine. I stole it from a teacher in Texas. She teaches five classes a day, and before each class, she puts a sticky note on the corner of her screen with just three things on it: the class name, today's date, and the file she's going to share. It takes about ten seconds to write, but it saves so much time. I use it myself now, at every training I run. Before that, I used to open the wrong slide deck all the time, and it was kind of embarrassing. Now I never lose track. Honestly, half of the best tips at these events come from teachers, not from us. I just collect them and pass them along. Once, I showed my vacation photos to two hundred teachers.
talks.gist: ダンさんのコツは、テキサスの先生から借りたアイデアで、画面のすみに貼るふせんです。クラス名と、その日の日付と、見せるファイルを書いておきます。

talks.en: Hi, I'm Chloe, from Hong Kong. I teach English, and once a month my students record themselves telling a short story. My favorite tip is a set of small cards with sentence starters, things like, one day, after that, or, in the end. Before we record, each student picks two or three cards and keeps them on their desk. It's such a small thing, but their recordings sound so much more confident. Before I started this, a lot of students just froze, or said um for ten seconds straight. Now they look at a card, and they keep going. I made the cards once, laminated them, and I've used the same set for two years now. Setup takes no time at all. I just hand them out. My quieter students especially love having something to hold on to.
talks.gist: クロエさんのコツは、話し始めのことばを書いたカードです。録音の前に2枚か3枚選んで、机に置いておきます。

talks.en: Hi, I'm Liam, from Vancouver. Every morning, my class does ten minutes of reading right when the bell rings, at eight forty-five. My favorite tip is a bookmark I made for that time. It's just a strip of paper with three questions on it, like, what's happening right now, or, who's your favorite character. Kids keep it inside their book. If they finish their book early, they pick one question and answer it in their reading notebook before they choose a new book. It keeps everyone reading quietly, instead of asking me what to do next. I've got twenty-two kids, so those ten minutes used to be pretty chaotic. Now it's actually the calmest part of my day. I printed a class set at the start of the year. It took about five minutes, and they still use the same ones. The rest of my day is not so calm.
talks.gist: リアムさんのコツは、3つの問いを書いた読書のしおりです。本を早く読み終えた子は、問いを1つ選んで、ノートに答えを書きます。

talks.en: Hello, I'm Wei, from Taichung. I teach geography at a high school, and we go on a field trip to the mountains or the coast twice a year. My favorite tip is really simple. Before the trip, I make one shared digital map, and I drop a pin on every stop, like where the bus parks, the lookout point, and the lunch spot. Students can see the whole route on their phones before we even leave school. It only takes about ten minutes to set up the night before. In the past, I just gave them a paper list, and they kept asking me where we were going next. Now they check the map themselves. And it works for any trip, not just geography. You just need a few pins and some short labels.
talks.gist: ウェイさんのコツは、遠足の前に、スマホで見られる地図を作っておくことです。バスをとめる場所や見晴らし台にピンを立てるだけで、準備は10分ほどです。

talks.en: Hi, I'm Emily, from Dublin. I'm a special education teacher, and my favorite tip is something small I use every single day. It's a laminated card with the word, first, on the left, and the word, then, on the right. I write or draw on it with a whiteboard marker, so it's different every time. First reading, then a break, for example. I hold it up, or I put it right on the student's desk. It takes about a minute to set up, because I just wipe it clean and write the next thing. For a student who gets anxious about what's coming next, seeing it really helps, more than just hearing me say it. It's not fancy at all, just a bit of laminated card and a marker. But I've used the same one for three years now, and I still reach for it every day.
talks.gist: エミリーさんのコツは、まず何をして、つぎに何をするかを書いて見せるカードです。書いて消せるので、準備は1分ほどです。

episodes.title: 写真と連絡先
episodes.topic: オンラインでの先生どうしのつながり
episodes.scene: エナジャイザーの、ふつかめの終わりです。アキは、ミアさんとカルロさんと、いっしょに写真をとります。そのあと、連絡先を交換して、このあとどうやってつながるかを話します。
episodes.q: カルロさんは、写真をどうやって送ると言っていましたか。
episodes.a: メールで送る、と言っていました。バイ・イーメール、です。それで、アキにアドレスを入れてもらっていました。

dialogue.en: Hey, before we all head off, let's take a picture together!
dialogue.ja: ねえ、みんな帰る前に、いっしょに写真をとりましょうよ。

dialogue.en: Yes, good idea! Can you get all three of us in?
dialogue.ja: いいですね。3人とも、ちゃんと入りますか。

dialogue.en: Sure, I've got long arms, you know. Okay, get closer. Say cheese!
dialogue.ja: まかせてください。ぼく、うでが長いんですよ。じゃあ、もっと寄って。はい、チーズ。

dialogue.en: Oh, that's a great one! Is it okay if I put it online later?
dialogue.ja: わあ、いい写真。あとで、ネットにのせてもいいですか。

dialogue.en: Sure, that's fine with me.
dialogue.ja: はい、いいですよ。

dialogue.en: Fine with me too. And Aki, I'll send it to you later, by email. Can you type your address in here?
dialogue.ja: ぼくもいいですよ。アキ、あとでメールで送りますね。ここにアドレスを入れてもらえますか。

dialogue.en: So, where can we find you online, Aki?
dialogue.ja: ところで、アキのことは、ネットのどこで見られますか。

dialogue.en: I have a website called School Stock.
dialogue.ja: スクール・ストックという、ウェブサイトをやっています。

dialogue.en: School Stock? Sorry, what's that?
dialogue.ja: スクール・ストック？ ごめんなさい、それって何ですか。

dialogue.en: It's a free website. I share worksheets and short animations.
dialogue.ja: 無料のサイトです。プリントや、短いアニメーションをのせています。

dialogue.en: Free? Aki, you're making the rest of us look bad.
dialogue.ja: 無料ですか。アキ、ぼくたちの立場がなくなりますよ。

dialogue.en: Ha! I'm just doing my best.
dialogue.ja: はは、精いっぱいやっているだけです。

dialogue.en: Oh, nice. I'll have a look when I get home.
dialogue.ja: いいですね。帰ったら、見てみます。

dialogue.en: Same here. And I'll put a link to my teacher group in the email, you know.
dialogue.ja: ぼくも見ますよ。メールに、ぼくの先生仲間のグループへのリンクも書いておきますね。

dialogue.en: Great. I'll check my email tonight.
dialogue.ja: よかった。今夜、メールを見ますね。

dialogue.en: Today was so much fun. I'm really glad we met, Aki.
dialogue.ja: きょうは、すごく楽しかったです。アキに会えて、ほんとうにうれしいです。

dialogue.en: Me too. Thanks for everything.
dialogue.ja: わたしもです。いろいろ、ありがとうございました。

dialogue.en: See you both tomorrow!
dialogue.ja: じゃあ、ふたりとも、またあした。

sounds.point: ロング・アームズ が ロンガームズ
sounds.natural: I've got long arms
sounds.clear: I've got long arms
sounds.explain: ロング の おわりの ング が、次の アームズ とつながって、ロンガームズ、に近く聞こえます。ふたつの語が、ひとつの語のように聞こえます。

sounds.point: プット・イット・オン が プリロン
sounds.natural: Is it okay if I put it online later?
sounds.clear: Is it okay if I put it online later?
sounds.explain: プット の ト と、イット の ト が、どちらも ら行に近い音になり、プリロンライン、に近く聞こえます。オーストラリアやアメリカの英語で、よく聞かれる音です。

sounds.point: センド・イット が センディッ
sounds.natural: I'll send it to you later, by email.
sounds.clear: I'll send it to you later, by email.
sounds.explain: センド の ド が、次の イット に つながって、センディッ、に近く聞こえます。イット の ト は、次の トゥ に のみこまれて、ほとんど聞こえないことが多いです。

joke.en: Free? Aki, you're making the rest of us look bad.

humor.why: 無料の教材サイトを作るアキさんを、ほかの先生の立場がなくなる、と軽くからかっています。中身はほめ言葉なので、ほめ言葉として受け取る、と返すのが合います。
humor.cue: けなすような言い方なのに、中身がほめ言葉で、話し手が笑っていたら、親しみのからかいです。

responses.en: Ha! I'm just doing my best.
responses.ja: はは、精いっぱいやっているだけです。
もう、やめてくださいよ。

aki.en: I'll take that as a compliment.
aki.ja: ほめ言葉として、受け取っておきます。

shower.topic_en: How I connect with teachers online

talks.en: Hi, I'm Mia, from Brisbane. Online, I mostly connect with other teachers through social media. I follow heaps of primary teachers, and I love seeing quick classroom tips, especially new ideas for little routines, like my morning check-in. Sometimes someone posts a photo of an activity, and I just try it the next day. I post a bit myself too, but only photos of things we've made, like our bean plants or our reading corner, never the kids' faces. Last month, I found a science teacher in Canada through one of those posts, and we've been messaging about how she teaches weather. We even had a quick Google Meet call last week. It's funny, we've never met in person, but I feel like I know her classroom already. Small ideas can travel a long way.
talks.gist: ミアさんは、エス・エヌ・エスで小学校の先生をたくさんフォローして、授業のヒントをもらっています。カナダの理科の先生とは、グーグル・ミートでも話しました。

talks.en: Hi, it's Carlo again, from Manila. Besides my local group of ICT teachers, I connect with people online too. I follow other ICT teachers on social media, and honestly, some of the best tips for teaching with only a few devices came from them, you know. I'm also in an online group for teachers who like doing video projects in class. We share short clips and ask each other questions, like, how did you get your students to edit that fast? Every couple of weeks, a few of us meet online after school, and one person shows a small trick. I mostly just listen and take notes. I don't post much myself. At this event, I'm hoping to meet a few more people, so I can keep learning after I go home.
talks.gist: カルロさんは、動画づくりが好きな先生の、オンラインのグループに入っています。2週間に1回くらい集まって、小さなこつを教え合っています。

talks.en: Hello, I'm Oliver, from London. I'm a trainer, so connecting with teachers online is a big part of my work. After every workshop, I send everyone a short email with the slides and a link to a shared Drive folder. Then, once a month, I run a free thirty-minute session on Google Meet, and teachers bring one question each. Quite often, it's the same question from three different countries, which I find rather lovely. I still hear from teachers months later, asking how to fix something, or just telling me what worked in their classroom. It reminds me that a slide in a training session doesn't mean much until someone actually uses it with real children. Honestly, the questions people send me afterwards are what keep me going. Usually, the question is, where did my file go?
talks.gist: オリバーさんは、研修のあとに資料をメールで送り、月に1回、30分の質問会をグーグル・ミートで開いています。

talks.en: Hi, I'm Jiwoo, from Busan. I studied in the U.S. for a while, so I still follow a lot of American teachers online. I like seeing how they set up their classrooms, and sometimes I borrow small ideas, like a reading corner or a job chart. I'm also in a small message group with teachers from other schools in Busan. We message each other about lesson ideas, especially before a big unit. It's nice having people to ask when something doesn't go well, because teaching can feel kind of lonely sometimes. With teachers I meet at events like this one, I usually swap emails, and then I send a short hello the next week, so we don't lose touch. I've already met a few people today, actually, and I really hope we keep talking.
talks.gist: ジウさんは、プサンのほかの学校の先生と、メッセージで授業の相談をしています。イベントで会った人には、次の週に短いあいさつのメールを送ります。

talks.en: Hi, I'm Arjun, from Pune. I teach physics, and I share a lab with two other science teachers, so we're used to talking in person. Online, I mostly follow physics teachers from other countries, just to see how they explain the same ideas differently. Once, a teacher in Brazil shared a short slow-motion video of a ball rolling down a ramp, and it gave me a much clearer way to explain motion. My students already film slow-motion videos on their phones, so the next week, we tried the same ramp in our lab. I also keep a list of email addresses from people I meet at events like this. It's useful, because I can write to them later with a specific question, like how to run an experiment with fewer materials. Sometimes my students find great videos before I do, and I don't mind that at all. They also find my old videos, which is less great.
talks.gist: アルジュンさんは、海外の物理の先生の教え方を見ています。ブラジルの先生の短い動画を見て、同じ坂の実験を、自分の実験室でもやってみました。

talks.en: Hi, I'm Rosa, from Cebu. I teach science at an elementary school, and online, I mostly follow other elementary teachers on social media. I like short, simple ideas, ones I can try the very next day without much preparation. I'm also in a small online group for science teachers. Once a week, someone posts a question, like, how do you keep young kids interested during a science lesson? People answer with real examples, not just theory, and that helps a lot. Last month, I asked how to grow plants in a classroom with no sunny window, and I got five good ideas in one day. Still, meeting people in person, like this week, feels different. It's really nice to finally put faces to the names I usually just read online.
talks.gist: ロサさんは、理科の先生のオンラインのグループで、次の日にすぐ試せるアイデアを集めています。先月は、1日で5つのアイデアがもらえたそうです。

episodes.title: 別れ際と、これから
episodes.topic: このイベントで学んだこと
episodes.scene: 最終日のわかれぎわです。アキは、ユーティンさん、ミンジュンさん、ミアさんと、次にオンラインで会う日と時間を決めます。
episodes.q: 次にオンラインで会うのは、なんようびの、なんじでしょう。
episodes.a: 来週の木曜日、夜8時です。ネクスト・サーズデイ、エイト・ピー・エム、と言っていました。アキは、火曜日のチューズデイとまちがえないように、聞き返していました。

dialogue.en: Aki, I can't believe it's already the last day.
dialogue.ja: アキ、もう最終日だなんて、信じられません。

dialogue.en: I know. It went by so fast.
dialogue.ja: ですよね。あっというまでした。

dialogue.en: It really did. Remember the first day? You were having a coffee, and we just sat down with you.
dialogue.ja: ほんとうに。初日のこと、覚えてますか。アキがコーヒーを飲んでいて、そこにわたしたちが座ったんですよね。

dialogue.en: Let's keep in touch after this, okay?
dialogue.ja: このあとも、連絡を取り合いましょうね。

dialogue.en: Definitely. I'd love to plan a lesson together.
dialogue.ja: ぜひ。いっしょに授業をつくりたいです。

dialogue.en: Me too. Remember, we talked about connecting our classes? Let's actually make it happen.
dialogue.ja: ぼくもです。クラスどうしをつなごうって、話しましたよね。ちゃんと形にしましょう。

dialogue.en: Okay. Should we have an online meeting?
dialogue.ja: はい。オンラインで打ち合わせをしましょうか。

dialogue.en: Sure. How about next Thursday, at eight p.m.?
dialogue.ja: いいですね。来週の木曜日、夜8時はどうですか。

dialogue.en: Sorry, Tuesday or Thursday?
dialogue.ja: すみません、火曜日ですか、木曜日ですか。

dialogue.en: Thursday. Next Thursday, at eight.
dialogue.ja: 木曜日です。来週の木曜日の、8時です。

dialogue.en: Got it. That works for me.
dialogue.ja: 分かりました。わたしも、それで都合がいいです。

dialogue.en: Good. Thursday, not Tuesday. Just like thirty, not thirteen.
dialogue.ja: そうです。木曜日で、火曜日じゃないですよ。サーティーンじゃなくて、サーティー、と同じですね。

dialogue.en: Ha! You remember that?
dialogue.ja: はは、覚えていたんですか。

dialogue.en: Perfect. Well, I've got to go. My flight's in two hours.
dialogue.ja: ばっちりですね。じゃあ、わたしはもう行かなくちゃ。フライトまで、あと2時間なんです。

dialogue.en: Okay. Have a safe flight, Mia.
dialogue.ja: はい。気をつけて帰ってくださいね、ミアさん。

dialogue.en: Thanks, Aki! Bye, everyone!
dialogue.ja: ありがとう、アキ。みんな、またね。

dialogue.en: Take care, Aki. See you soon.
dialogue.ja: お元気で、アキさん。また近いうちに。

dialogue.en: Thank you so much. I'm still learning English, but I'm so glad we talked.
dialogue.ja: ほんとうに、ありがとうございました。英語はまだ勉強中ですが、みなさんと話せて、とてもうれしかったです。

sounds.point: キープ・イン が キーピン
sounds.natural: Let's keep in touch.
sounds.clear: Let's keep in touch.
sounds.explain: キープ の プ が、うしろの イン とつながって、キーピン・タッチ、に近く聞こえます。キープ と イン のあいだに、ウ の音は、ほとんどはいりません。

sounds.point: シー・ユー が シーヤ
sounds.natural: See ya soon.
sounds.clear: See you soon.
sounds.explain: ユー が弱く短くなって、ヤ、に近い音になります。シーヤ・スーン、とひと続きに聞こえます。

sounds.point: ガット・トゥー が ガタ
sounds.natural: I've gotta go.
sounds.clear: I've got to go.
sounds.explain: ガット・トゥー が ひとつになって、アイヴ・ガタ・ゴー、に近く聞こえます。ミアさんの発音では、ゴタ、に近く聞こえるかもしれません。

joke.en: Good. Thursday, not Tuesday. Just like thirty, not thirteen.

humor.why: 第一回で、サーティーとサーティーンを聞き返した場面を、最後の日に思い出させています。いっしょに過ごした時間があるから笑える、仲間の冗談です。
humor.cue: 前に出てきた言い回しと同じ形の言葉が、別の場面でくり返されたら、前の話を拾う冗談です。

responses.ja: はは、覚えていたんですか。

aki.en: Thirty, not thirteen. I'll never forget that.
aki.ja: サーティーンじゃなくて、サーティー。ずっと忘れません。

shower.topic_en: What I learned at this event

talks.en: Hi everyone, I'm Yu-ting, from Taipei. The biggest thing I learned at this event is that teachers everywhere care about the same things, even in very different classrooms. I teach English and computer science from first grade to sixth grade, so I'm always looking for new ideas. One session showed how to make short picture stories with Slides, and I think my younger students would love that. I also went to a workshop about feedback in pairs. The idea is simple. Each student says one thing they like, and asks one question. My sixth graders are almost done with their recycling game, and next month they're showing it to the fourth graders, so I want to try this feedback idea then. Honestly, talking with teachers from so many countries made me feel a lot less alone in this job.
talks.gist: ユーティンさんは、スライドで短い絵のお話を作る方法と、ペアで、いいところと質問を伝え合うやりかたを持ち帰ります。いろいろな国の先生と話せて、心強かったそうです。

talks.en: Hello, I'm Min-jun, from Seoul. When I came here, I mainly wanted new ideas for group work, and I got more than I expected. I teach science to five classes, about thirty students each, and we do at least one experiment every week, in groups of four. In one workshop, a teacher showed how her students write their own questions on a shared slide before an experiment. Then the class votes on which question to test. That fits my goal this year, letting students ask their own questions, not just answer mine. I also talked with a few teachers about quiet students in group work. One idea was to give each person in the group a clear job, like reader, recorder, or timekeeper. I'm going to try both ideas with one class first, and see how my students respond.
talks.gist: ミンジュンさんは、実験の前に生徒が自分で問いを書き、どれを確かめるかをみんなで決める方法を知りました。グループのひとりひとりに役割をもたせる案も試すそうです。

talks.en: Hi, I'm Mia, from Brisbane. For me, the best part of this event was hearing how other teachers start their day. I do a quick one-word check-in with my Year Three class every morning, and I picked up heaps of new ideas for it here. One teacher lets her kids pick a colour instead of a word, which is great for the shy ones. I also learned a simple way to keep our shared Chromebooks organised. My class shares a set with the class next door, and honestly, it gets kind of messy. Kind of messy is a polite way to say it. Another teacher showed me how she sets up folders in Drive, one for each student, so the kids can find their own work quickly. I'm going to try that as soon as I get back. But what I'll remember most is how many people here really love this job, even when it's hard.
talks.gist: ミアさんは、グーグル・ドライブでひとりずつフォルダを作る整理のしかたを、帰ってすぐ試すそうです。いちばん心に残ったのは、大変でもこの仕事が好きな人が、たくさんいたことです。

talks.en: G'day, I'm Jack, from Melbourne. I came to this event hoping to find two or three things I could use straight away, and I've definitely got them. I teach maths at a secondary school, and one session on using Sheets for quick checks during a lesson was really useful. Students answer a couple of questions, and you can see right away who's falling behind. I'm going to try it with my next unit. But honestly, what I'll remember most is the chats between sessions. I met teachers from at least six countries, and a couple of them want to try my spaghetti bridge project with their classes. That's what makes these events worth it, you know. I'm heading home with a full notebook and way too many ideas. My GEG group's going to hear about every single one, whether they like it or not.
talks.gist: ジャックさんは、グーグル・シートを使って、授業中にさっと理解を確かめる方法を持ち帰ります。なんにんかの先生が、スパゲッティの橋づくりを、それぞれのクラスでやってみたいそうです。

talks.en: Hello, I'm Wei Ling, from Singapore. I came here mostly curious about how other teachers make maths feel real for young kids. I teach Primary Four, and we already use paper pizzas for fractions, but I picked up a few new hands-on ideas, like measuring things around the school with string. One teacher showed a simple way to record students explaining their thinking on Slides, so parents can see the steps, not just the answer. I really liked that, because in my class, explaining is part of the score. I also enjoyed comparing class sizes with other teachers. Mine has thirty-two students, and I got some good tips for pairing students during group talk. I'm leaving with a much longer list of ideas than I expected, and the recording idea is right at the top.
talks.gist: ウェイリンさんがいちばん試したいのは、子どもが考えかたを説明するようすを、スライドに記録する方法です。答えだけでなく、そこまでの道すじも、保護者に見てもらえます。

talks.en: Hey, I'm Sam, from Wellington. I teach English at a secondary school, and I came here mainly for the sessions on feedback. The best one was about getting students to use a rubric on their own work before they hand it in. It's simple, and they fix a lot of small things themselves, so I can spend my marking time on the bigger stuff. I also picked up an idea for my quieter students. They record themselves reading a short paragraph, listen back, and then try again. Nobody else has to hear it, so it feels safe. I'm keen to start that next week. I also had some good chats about marking speaking tasks fairly, which I've never felt confident about. It was good to hear I'm not the only one. Coming here on my own felt a bit strange at first, but by the end, it didn't feel that way at all. Now I've got so many new friends, I'll need a spreadsheet.
talks.gist: サムさんは、生徒が提出する前に、自分でルーブリックを使って見直す方法を持ち帰ります。おとなしい生徒には、自分の音読を録音して聞き直す活動を試すそうです。
